#2716. John Harbaugh: Cam Skattebo was not supposed to push on Jameis Winston sneak

Giants coach John Harbaugh defended running back Cam Skattebo, who stayed in his stance on a crucial Jameis Winston quarterback sneak during Thursday night’s loss to the Commanders.

Harbaugh said the call was a quarterback sneak but not a tush push, and Skattebo wasn’t supposed to be pushing Winston.

“We had a certain check involved in it, so he wasn’t supposed to be up there pushing. We didn’t call the same [QB sneak] that we’ve been calling,” Harbaugh said, via Pat Leonard of the New York Daily News. “What else am I supposed to say? He wasn’t supposed to be up there pushing.”

Why the Giants wouldn’t want Skattebo to push Winston in an attempt to get the first down yardage is unclear, but the play looked strange, and it was a big one for the Giants, who had a 21-17 lead late in the fourth quarter at the time, but couldn’t hold the lead after getting stuffed on that quarterback sneak and lost 24-21.

#2711. Purdue 80 Ohio 62: Post Game Presser

The Purdue Boilermakers looked like a team that is improving over the first several weeks of the season as they picked up a victory against the Ohio Bobcats 80-62. After being moved the bench, Gicarri Harris showed is scoring ability as he 8-12 from the floor for 23 points, 5 rebounds, 4 assists, and steals even after starting his night with an airball.

Antoine Harris had another stellar game even though he did not get a chance to start following being late to a film session ahead of the game. The freshman ended with 17 points, 3 rebounds, 4 assists, and a steal. The Boilers, on the backs of Harris, West, and Cox's 16 points and 4 rebounds, were able to recover from a lackluster start to the second half that pulled the game to 43-36 with 15:30 remaining in the second half.

Head Coach Matt Painter and players Gicarri Harris, Antoine West, and Enzo Shahrvin share their thoughts following the victory for the Boilers to even their season record at 2-2.

Painter is working to figure out his team in the early part of the season more so than he has needed to over the last several seasons. He spoke a lot about consistency from his team, noting that the team has had good stretches in the first half of games but then seem to make things difficult for themselves by going away from what was working and taking difficult shots. He would eventually bring up that players have got to figure out some things as their youth is showing at times, especially doing individual things and not team first type of things.

Predetermined thoughts. It seems to be where some of the guys who are struggling are playing with where they think the ball should go or having their mind made up ahead of time instead of playing reactive to what the defense is going them. Some guys have got to not simply take shots because they want to take shots.

Something you don't often hear from Painter but he verbalized some frustration from guys not making enough effort plays. He said there were some plays where guys needed to get on the floor and they just didn't. If the indications from former players still hold true, that'll be taken care of in the next few practices.

Consistency seems to be the key word so far through four games. Painter stated he needed consistency from individual players but also from groups of players. I'm sure he was likely speaking directly to Cox and Harris as those guys are veteran guards who need to be playing at a high level consistently for everyone else to play better. As a group, Painter may have been speaking to his groupings of players once the starters aren't on the floor together.

West was late to a film session but it seems pretty clear that Painter is going to go with Ertel, Cox, West, Benter, and DJ at some point to start the game. That's about a consistent of a group as CMP can put on the floor but it also gives him some options coming off the bench in how to work his lineup, especially as Enzo continues to improve and get a feel for what Purdue needs and wants from him.

Speak of Enzo, the French big man looked vastly improved from what we saw against UCONN and even from earlier in the week against Illinois State. He didn't score in this game but he did some great things, notably CMP mentioning his gortats (interior seals on drives) and his improvement in knowing how to recover following his ball screen defense. As he continues to figure out what he can and can't do in the college game and as he gets more comfortable with his teammates, he'll continue to help Purdue win games.

Harris gave some insight during his moment in the media session and said that Enzo is a very unselfish player but he is learning to start scoring more when the opportunities are presented to him. That's going to likely come from rebounds and opportunities in transition. Enzo moves at an elite level for a player his size and once he figures out how the college game, he will take a big leap forward in providing Purdue with some uniqueness.

Painter noted how well Harris practiced leading up to the game against Ohio. Although the move to the bench may have been a bit of a reality check for the junior guard and allowed him to refocus, Painter said that he wasn't practicing poorly before but it was very much so noticeable that he was practicing at a high level. He deserves to start for what he has done for the program and his own personal sacrifices, but Purdue may be better with him coming off the bench. He played so well in that first half, CMP rewarded him with a second half start.

Following a question from Dustin Schuette of Sports Illustrated about maintaining focus and process based when things aren't going well, Matt Painter said that is THE battle they are facing offensively. CMP stated: 'We have good pieces. We have talented guys. We have some youthfulness and you see that come out and that is where that inconsistency comes from. You've got to trust what you work on every day.'

Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford celebrates a touchdown against the Washington Commanders on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026, in Landover, Maryland. Getty Images

Los Angeles Rams tight end Tyler Higbee celebrates a first down against the Buffalo Bills in Inglewood, Calif., Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. AP Photo/Scott Strazzante

#2696. 49ers-Cowboys preview: Christian McCaffrey and the Niners should run wild

History will lead you in the right direction more often than not. The head-to-head matchups between the San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys have been one-sided. It's why it's a rivalry in name only.

How the 49ers have fared against the NFC East and the Cowboys versus the NFC West is more evidence of what to expect this coming Sunday. The Niners have been terrific in that regard, while Dallas has gone 2-5 in their previous seven games — including a loss to the Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew-led Cardinals, in a game in which they allowed 30 points.

Let's preview Week 10's matchup to see whether Dak Prescott can keep pace with Brock Purdy.

Purdy is 3-0 in his career against the Cowboys. His fourth start against Dallas might be the biggest mismatch, at least on this side of the ball, to date. The 49ers are top-three offensively in points per game, EPA per pass, EPA per rush, passing and rushing success rate, and in third-down and red-zone efficiency.

Conversely, the Cowboys are bottom-five or worst in total yards and rushing yards per game, EPA per play and rush, sacks per game, and third-down efficiency. Dallas's saving grace on this side of the ball is that they are sixth in turnover EPA per game.

Down-to-down, they've been lousy. The Cowboys give up a league-high 35.2 yards per opponent possession. After a mid-season quarterback change, Arizona had drives of 70, 80, 58, and 90 yards before a 44-yard game-winning field goal drive in overtime.

Quinnen Williams is one of the NFL's best interior linemen. He's the ultimate disruptor. Williams leads all defensive tackles with 14 tackles for loss—five more than Jeffery Simmons. His five sacks are tied for third. The 18 run stops are tied for third. Yet, for whatever reason, the Cowboys have been abysmal against the inside run.

When you watch them, the issues stem from getting moved at the point of attack. Ball carriers aren't getting touched until they cross the line of scrimmage. The eye test matches the stats: Dallas allows the second-most yards before contact per carry this season, at 1.78 yards. They get moved, easily, despite having played only two offenses in the top-15 in rushing success rate.

The 49ers are running more and more inside the tackles. They're running inside zone at a 19.1% clip, a slight increase from a year ago. This game sets up well for the Niners to keep attacking the Cowboys' A and B gaps.

Kyle Shanahan had to be grinning as he watched the 36-play reel of the Cowboys' defense defending —a term used loosely—inside zone. They allowed 8.08 yards per carry. Seven of those 36 plays went for double digits. They allowed a 58.3% success rate.

You could build the case that the 49ers aren't running inside enough this season. Christian McCaffrey had two 11-yard runs on inside zone last week. McCaffrey has 24 inside zone carries this year and averages 5.04 yards per carry, with a 62.5% success rate.

Add in the different motions and window dressing, and it's tough to see the defense that allowed the best rushing attack (Tampa Bay) its face this season to run for 241 yards slow down the 49ers.

Trent Williams injured his shoulder in practice and is questionable. Veteran Vederian Lowe would take Williams' place if he cannot suit up.

As big a loss as that would be for the 49ers, the Cowboys are 29th in stuff rate. They do not get stops on the ground. Their linebackers get caught up in the wash, creating massive rushing lanes.

The Cowboys allow a good amount of chunk plays through the air. They're 27th in EPA per pass. They're also 25th in passing success rate.

Watching Daniel Jones forgo intermediate passes last week for underneath throws was maddening. Receivers were open. They just weren't targeted.

How has Dallas held up against elite passing offenses? C.J. Stroud threw for 347 yards. Nico Collins and Jaylin Noel each had over 85 receiving yards. Jordan Love threw for 276 yards. Matthew Golden and Christian Watson combined for nine catches and 168 yards.

No Mike Evans again for the 49ers, but this should not be a defense where the Niners need their No. 1 target. The Cowboys don't create negative plays. What Purdy will see this week compared to next is the polar opposite—the Cowboys blitz 20.2% of the time, the second-lowest mark in the league.

In theory, Purdy should have plenty of time to scan the field and pick Dallas apart. It's a Vic Fangio-adjacent defense, so the Cowboys will do all they can to take away the middle of the field and funnel targets to lower-percentage areas, like outside the numbers.

Jordan Watkins has ten targets in the previous two games. Cornerback Joey Porter Jr. looks set to return from injury and will look to slow down Watkins hot streak.

Rookie Caleb Downs is the player the Niners could find success against. He's primarily played nickel. Against the Texans, Packers, and Cardinals, Downs allowed all 9 of his targets to be completed for 147 yards.

Heading into Week 9, Downs had allowed a 90.5% completion percentage, which was the third-highest among slot cornerbacks this season. He has one pass breakup. Dallas tried to align him closer to the line of scrimmage, almost like a pseudo-linebacker in coverage against Arizona. He played linebacker 32.1% of the time against the Cardinals. But now he's facing an offense that thrives over the middle. Downs has nowhere to hide against the Niners.

Old friend Kendrick Bourne caught a slant on Downs, broke a tackle, and gained a bunch of yards en route to a 29-yard gain. Downs was no match for Trey McBride on a 3rd-and-6 target— hello, George Kittle.

Downs is not a big player. He's 5'11", 206 pounds, but has a 10th percentile arm length. That shows up in contested situations when he can't make plays on the ball.

Savion Williams from the Packers got Downs a couple of times on in-breaking routes. Watson and Golden each had a double-digit reception against Watkins on an out route on third down.

He would've allowed two first-down receptions on third down last week to the Colts, but his brother dropped the ball both times. You better believe the rookie will be on the 49ers' radar.

Whether it's the No. 1, 2, or slot receiver, the Cowboys are bottom-three in yards after the catch allowed per reception. The No. 2 third-down offense meets the 32nd third-down defense. The No. 1 red zone offense meets the No. 25 red zone defense. Dallas also has six more defensive penalties than the 31st-placed team.

On paper, the only thing stopping the 49ers from scoring in this game is the 49ers. Outside of Quinnen Williams, this defense has zero redeeming qualities.

The 49ers forced five turnovers, masking the Raiders' six potential scoring drives.

Luck plays a role in every turnover. To date, the Cowboys are 22nd in turnover EPA lost per game on offense. They make mistakes. Look no further than last week when Dak Prescott fumbled on third down, or CeeDee Lamb fumbled going into score.

Fred Warner and the Niners defense have a penchant for the peanut punch. They're sixth this year at forcing fumbles, thanks in large part to the soon-to-be Defensive Player of the Year.

Starting cornerbacks Renardo Green and Deommodore Lenoir practiced Friday for the first time. Nate Hobbs practiced in full and could make his debut, especially with Upton Stout banged up. It'll be all hands on deck to slow down the most potent offense on the schedule yet.

Raheem Morris has been a godsend for this organization. He's developed a scheme that is third at limiting explosive plays and fifth in yards per attempt. The biggest surprise is the 49ers being first in EPA per rush this season.

Warner plays a significant role in limited targets over the middle. Teams are terrified to throw the ball between the numbers at 5 and 15 yards. The 49ers have allowed 31 yards per game, the best in the NFL. Their explosive play rate of 5% is also the league-leading rate. That's better than 9% of the league average.

But this will be the first team in the top 8 in EPA per pass that the defense has faced. No Jake Ferguson is a big blow; Lamb, George Pickens, and Ryan Flournoy provide plenty of firepower.

Another area the 49ers have been fantastic at is taking away throws to the slot. The Niners allow slot receivers a 51% target share, good for second-lowest in the league. All the post-snap spinning they do at safety, paired with that Warner guy lurking, forces the quarterback to throw outside the numbers. It's worked to date, but there haven't been a Lamb and Pickens on the outside, either.

The best receiver the 49ers faced this season, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, had 102 yards on five catches. Brock Bowers had 111 receiving yards last week. Trey McBride had 75 yards back in September. Those are the three players the team's game plan is built around, and the Niners failed to stop any of them.

It'd be a breath of fresh air to see the Niners' cornerbacks be competitive in this spot. One thing they have going for them is the game script. The Cowboys may not want to run the ball against San Francisco, even if it's great on great. Dallas is fifth in rushing success rate. But you won't run the ball if you're constantly trailing on the scoreboard.

Prescott, like Kirk Cousins, does not take sacks. This season, the 49ers lead the league in sack percentage on offense at 3%. The Raiders are right behind them at 3.2%. Dallas ranks fifth at 3.8%. Dallas is also eighth in pressure rate allowed.

Things change when the run threat no longer exists. The Niners' defensive line feasts on obvious passing downs. Osa Odighizuwa gets a shot at redemption from the team that traded him. Keion White and Romello Height get to pin their ears back, while veterans DeForest Buckner and Nick Bosa get their second game together.

When you filter to players with at least 350 passing snaps, the Cowboys tackles rank third and fourth in the highest blown-block rate in the NFL at 5.3% and 5.2%, with a combined eight sacks. For reference, Colton McKivitz has a blown-block rate of 2.3%, and Trent Williams is at 2%.

The 49ers were built to play with a lead and harass one-dimensional offenses. Dallas will score. They'll probably score a lot. But Prescott will be under pressure to keep pace with Purdy.

San Francisco isn't the only team stepping up in class. The Cowboys scored 20 points against the Giants in Week 1, but failed to surpass 17 points against the two other playoff defenses they faced this season. It might be premature to assume that'll change against a defense ranked sixth in the NFL in points allowed per game.

The Cowboys can hurt you on third down (5th) and in the red zone (3rd). The only area outside of sacks where the Niners are below league average is on third downs. One turnover. One punt. One mishap. That's all it's taken so far this season, and that'll likely continue for the 49ers on the road against a team with high expectations coming into the year, but that has failed to live up to the talent. (Something we never say about the Cowboys.)

#2694. At least 50 different quarterbacks will have started games through Week 10

Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza will make his first career start on Sunday. Two others will make their debuts, too: Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck and Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord.

Via NBC Sports research, they’ll become the 48th, 49th, and 50th different quarterbacks to start games during the 2026 season.

It will be only the second time in the last 15 years (excluding the 1987 strike season) during which 50 different quarterbacks have started games in the first 10 weeks of a season.

If, for some reason, another quarterback makes his first start of the season on Sunday (that’s unlikely with Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock not having an injury designation for Sunday), it will be the second-most starters through 10 weeks since 1950.

In 1999, 55 different quarterbacks started games through the first 10 weeks of the season.

Most of the changes have arisen from injury. For the Raiders, the transition to Mendoza happened after Kirk Cousins was traded to the Vikings.

#2693. Jets offense trying to move past massive ‘what-ifs’ as they finally get true opportunity to shine

It's hard not to ruminate over what could have been.

Garrett Wilson and Breece Hall, two of the faces of the Jets franchise, have hardly spent any time on the field together this season. Wilson is expected to be cleared from the concussion protocol, coach Aaron Glenn said Friday, and be available for Sunday's game against the Bills at MetLife Stadium.

He is listed as questionable but was a full participant in Friday's practice. It would be the first time the Jets have both Wilson and Hall since their Week 3 loss to the Lions on Sept. 27.

Another Jets season has spiraled away from them in between.

"Yeah, it's a lot of what-ifs that we talk about," Hall told The Post after practice Friday. "But at the end of the day, you gotta snap back to reality and live in the present. The present is we gotta find a way to win."

The Jets' talented group of playmakers in Wilson, Hall, Omar Cooper Jr., Adonai Mitchell, Kenyon Sadiq and Mason Taylor — with a competent quarterback in Geno Smith and strong offensive line to utilize them — was a big reason there was genuine optimism before the year. The group had the potential to create a dynamic offense after years of ineptitude. On paper, plenty of teams would sign up for that kind of offensive firepower.

New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) fails to complete a reception against Las Vegas Raiders cornerback Eric Stokes (5) on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Bill Kostroun for NY nPost

But that group was quickly disrupted and hasn't had a chance to show its full strength. Sunday could be the first time since the season opener that the full complement of offensive weapons is available.

And really, since the first drive of the opener, as Cooper suffered from a sprained ankle on the seventh offensive play of the season.

Cooper missed Weeks 2-5 with the injury. Mitchell missed Weeks 3-6 with a finger injury. Hall was out for Weeks 4-8 with a quad injury. And once Hall returned last week in the loss to the Chiefs, Wilson was out with the concussion he sustained the week prior in a loss to the Raiders.

It's likely they will now all finally get their chance. Cooper (ankle) and Mitchell (knee) are both listed as questionable for Sunday, though they were full participants in Friday's practice and Glenn indicated they will play.

If there is something left for Jets fans to watch this season, it's how this group looks together.

"It's good to see all those men getting a chance to be on the field," Glenn said. "But I will continue to say this: There's only one ball, and I wish there were more than that because those guys are extremely talented and they have the capabilities of making not just big plays, but able to sustain drives for us by the way they operate. Again, I look forward to having all those guys out there. I know they look forward to it, and I know Geno does too."

Breece Hall runs the ball during an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on Nov. 8, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. Getty Images

It's likely too late for the Jets to save this season and play any meaningful football the rest of the way. But it's an opportunity for this offense to establish itself ahead of next year — Wilson, Hall, Mitchell, Cooper, Sadiq and Taylor are all under contract for next year. If the Jets fire Glenn and are in a head coach search next offseason, it could be something that entices potential candidates.

"It's a great opportunity," Hall said. "I think we have some very winnable games. We've lost five one-score games, so I think teams know we're good and capable of it. It's all about finishing."

Finishing in the red zone has been the main struggle holding the Jets offense back so far this year. They've moved the ball well in their own half before falling apart when it matters most.

A full-strength unit could help in that area.

"I feel like we can be one of the top-tier offenses in the league," Hall said, "for sure."

#2690. John Harbaugh breaks down key — and controversial — moments from Giants loss

Cam Skattebo didn't just forget to push the tush.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh explained Friday that the failed third-and-1 quarterback sneak by Jameis Winston late in the fourth quarter was not a traditional Tush Push and thus it was not detrimental that it took Skattebo nearly two seconds to fire out of his pre-snap stance.

"That was a different kind of play, that was a normal quarterback sneak," Harbaugh said. "It had a certain check involved in it that is part of the play so he wasn't supposed to be up there pushing."

Perhaps the clearest evidence that it is not a cover-up is that fullback Patrick Ricard was lined up as a tight end and not pushing Winston, either.

New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo reacts on the bench during the second quarter against the Washington Commanders, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Charles Wenzelberg/NY Post

The failed third-down conversion led to the now-infamous "Who let the dogs out?" cadence on fourth-and-1 at the 11-yard line.

"It's not about what you say, exactly," Harbaugh said. "While it was, I think, probably fun on his part, the way the cadence sounds was an attempt to draw him offsides. That they would hear something different. They are going to jump based on the fact that they are too antsy and as soon as they hear the word and anticipate the snap, they are going to jump. They are not trying to define the word you said."

New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston (19) warms up before an NFL football game against the Washington Commanders in East Rutherford, N.J., Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Getty Images

Harbaugh said that in hindsight he wouldn't have wasted time with the trickery and taking a delay of game penalty that backed up punter Jordan Stout.

"If I had to do it again, I wouldn't even try to do it," Harbaugh said. "It didn't end up hurting us in the end. They are probably not going to jump there. [The Commanders] are a team that's jumped offside a bunch in those situations. They probably have been emphasizing it to a high degree, and they weren't budging."

"You say, 'Who let the dogs out?' and then you snap the ball," Harbaugh said. "Maybe that would've been a better strategy."

Snap the ball at the 11-yard line while protecting a four-point lead? That's Lions head coach Dan Campbell-levels of gutsy.

"I'm kind of kicking myself," Harbaugh said. "Maybe we should've gone for that one. You can kind of get as aggressive as you want. We're not afraid. We've done that before [in Baltimore]. History would tell you that."

New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh speaks during a press conference after an NFL football game in East Rutherford, N.J., Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. AP Photo/Seth Wenig

All six of kicker Dominic Zvada's missed field goals this season have come from the right hash.

"There is a technique issue there with his plant foot that we're looking at," Harbaugh said. "He needs to clean that up from a consistency standpoint. There is an issue on the right hash, no question."

The Giants punted three times across midfield: Fourth-and-12 at the 42-yard line, fourth-and-3 at the 46 and fourth-and-5 at the 41.

"When we were talking about them during the game, we just felt like they were out of range to go for it," Harbaugh said. "A lot of it was the analytics. But even feeling comfortable about doing it. We may be more aggressive in the future than we were."

#2689. Jayson Tatum won't give air to Jaylen Brown drama ahead of Celtics-Sixers game: 'Another game on the schedule'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- Jayson Tatum downplayed Tuesday's showdown between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which will be the first time that he and former teammate Jaylen Brown will face each other as opponents.

"It's another game on the schedule. It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one," Tatum said after putting up 21 points, four rebounds and six assists in a 117-97 win over the Milwaukee Bucks. "This one counted as one. Go get ready for Tuesday. It's a really good team, obviously. Incredible group, great coaching staff, they've been playing really well. So from that standpoint it's gonna be fun. But it's nothing more than Celtics versus Sixers."

Tatum and Brown spent nine seasons together, and led the Celtics to the 2024 championship -- the historic franchise's first since 2008 and record-setting 18th overall -- before the latter was traded to Philadelphia this summer in a blockbuster deal that brought Paul George to Boston.

Much has been made about Tatum and Brown's relationship, or lack thereof, particularly over the last few weeks.

Late last month, Tatum shared his recollection of the trade in an episode of his documentary series, "Summer of Jayson." "I was just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world," he said. In the comment section of the clip online, Brown called "cap."

Shortly after, Tatum tried to shut down any drama by pointing to all that they had accomplished together. "This ain't no f---in' Shaq and Kobe, there's no beef," Tatum said. "It's not about that. It should be more praise, and I understand that don't necessarily sell. Drama gets clicks and views, but I'm not really — that's not my thing."

Brown, on the other hand, played into the drama a few days later. "There's no beef," Brown said. "Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. It's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chop. And some gravy. He should stay ready at all times."

Now, as the first meeting between the former teammates arrives, both have tried to keep the focus on basketball.

"It's nothing to talk about. I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said after the 76ers secured a 127-121 win over the Chicago Bulls on Sunday. "Just playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win, so it's nothing to talk about. Just check the ball up. ... "We'll see how I feel when we get out there, but as of now, I got no emotion towards anything. So I'm just ready to go."

When Tatum asked if he would have a conversation with Brown on Tuesday, his response was a simple "I'm not able to tell the future," before adding that he had "no idea" if any such conversation would have to wait until after the season.

"I just know that it's the Celtics versus the Sixers. Just go out there and do my job and try to get another win," Tatum said. "Get through that, got a game on Wednesday. It's a long season. We got 72 games left. That's just the focus right now."

As for the actual basketball, both players and teams are off to terrific starts. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists on 47.7% shooting, including 39.2% from 3-point range, for the 9-2 Sixers, who sit atop the Eastern Conference. Tatum, meanwhile, is at 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists for the 8-2 Celtics, who are alone in second.

#2686. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Luka's Lakers look amazing, are Hornets regretting LaMelo trade?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

At the risk of tempting fate, we're coming off of a pretty optimistic week in the NBA. The late-October rush of season-altering injuries has seemingly slowed down. The quality of basketball has been excellent, and stars are making history. Things in the NBA are so positive right now that there are multiple, ongoing seven-game winning streaks that won't be featured in our winners of the week.

So... who beat out the trimmed-for-space Golden State Warriors and San Antonio Spurs? And who are our losers in a week full of winners? Let's dive into our rankings from the week that was.

No Jalen Williams. No Cason Wallace. No Chet Holmgren. And also, no losses. That's the week that the Thunder just had, first sweeping their season series with the Cleveland Cavaliers before blowing the doors off of the Memphis Grizzlies and Washington Wizards by 70 combined points. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander averaged just under 36 points in the 4-0 stretch, but the story here is Oklahoma City finding a new formula to compensate for all of these absences.

The Thunder built their historic defense around turnover generation, leading the NBA on that front in their 2025 championship season and finishing No. 2 a year ago. They've fallen to 21st as of Sunday, accepting that they simply cannot play as aggressively without their core defenders as they once did. Instead, they're selling out to protect the basket. They allowed the second-fewest points in the paint per game a season ago ... and have trimmed five of them off of their average this season. They've even started Isaiah Hartenstein and Aday Mara together in two of their past three games, though they've shared minimal possessions.

The defense may not be generating turnovers, but the offense isn't committing any either. Oklahoma City has taken its turnover-prevention offense to the extreme. The Thunder are averaging 231.6 passes per game, 10 fewer than any team in the tracking era. Only the Spurs and the Philadelphia 76ers, both healthy championship contenders, are turning the ball over less. This "no passes means no turnovers" offense only works if the individual creators are up to snuff. Gilgeous-Alexander obviously fits the bill, but now, so does Ajay Mitchell. The Thunder are scoring over 1.2 points per possession when Mitchell shoots out of pick-and-roll, good for the 94th percentile league-wide. He's scoring just under 25 points per 36 minutes, more than Cade Cunningham and just below Deni Avdija and Austin Reaves.

Oh yeah, and they made a trade with the Sacramento Kings. I'm comfortable calling any team lucky enough to trade with the Kings an automatic winner for that week, especially when they're acquiring a guard on a rookie contract. Do the words "Tyrese Haliburton" mean nothing to you, Sacramento? Nique Clifford certainly won't live up to that prematurely dealt King, but there's a parallel here to Davion Mitchell, another former first-round pick the Kings dealt who has since blossomed with the Miami Heat. You should trust no team's ability to evaluate players less than Sacramento's ... and no team's more than Oklahoma City's. If Sam Presti thinks Clifford can help the injury-ravaged Thunder, I'm inclined to believe that a price of two second-round picks is a bargain. All in all, it was about as perfect a week as the Thunder could have asked for.

He's averaging 40 points! This isn't a handful of games against terrible teams anymore. The Portland Trail Blazers have been great defensively against everyone except the Los Angeles Lakers because Luka has blitzed them for 94 points in two meetings. Of the 20 highest individual point totals so far this season, Dončić comes in at No. 1, No. 2, No. 5, No. 12, No. 17 and No. 18. The two biggest pillars of the MVP race are scoring and winning. Clearly, he's got the scoring down.

So far, winning hasn't been an issue either. The Lakers are 9-2, and it's almost exclusively because of the offense he runs. As of Sunday, the Lakers ranked 23rd in rebounding rate, 23rd in defense and 25th in turnover rate. It hasn't mattered because the offense is No. 1 with a bullet. The Lakers are roughly 34 points per 100 possessions better when he plays than when he sits, yet they were still able to pull off a critical road win over the Detroit Pistons on Sunday without him. The Lakers are a regular-season wins machine, and Dončić is the engineer.

It's not just the raw total, either. It's how this is all happening. Dončić currently leads the NBA in both 3-point attempts and free-throw attempts. When James Harden was doing that a decade ago, it was considered such witchcraft that defenders started standing behind him and guarding him with their hands behind their backs. I look forward to seeing what sort of nonsense teams concoct against Dončić if this continues. He's making 30-footers look like layups. He's giving Laker fans the sort of individual offense they haven't seen since Kobe Bryant's peak. Enjoy it. Stretches like this don't come around often.

The underlying message of the Ball trade was that the Charlotte Hornets did not think he could be relied upon as a franchise player. Given the questions surrounding his durability, his defense and even his maturity, it wasn't a crazy thought. The idea that he would fare better in a secondary role in Minnesota made plenty of sense. He and Anthony Edwards looked like one of the NBA's best duos in the season's opening week. Then Edwards got hurt, and Ball was suddenly back to being the centerpiece. How has he responded? Well, let's look at the team numbers since Edwards went down:

It's a tiny sample, but thus far, Ball is impacting his new Timberwolves teammates in much the same way he affected his former Hornets (don't worry, we'll get to them!). Everyone else's life gets vastly simpler on offense when they're fortunate enough to play with LaMelo Ball. Even without Edwards, he's more than kept the Timberwolves afloat. When Edwards eventually returns, this team is a genuine contender in the Western Conference.

With Ball, the Hornets had the best offense in the NBA from early December through the end of last season. Well, without him, they're last. By a mile. They're last in basically everything. No team has a lower true shooting percentage. No team turns the ball over. Ready for a jarring stat? We covered Oklahoma City's "no pass" offense earlier. Well, the Thunder are averaging more assists than the Hornets this season ... on 65 fewer passes per game.

The Hornets knew they were getting worse when they made the trade. It was a conscious choice: take a step back, take a few spins in the revamped lottery, accumulate assets that could be flipped later. The Hornets felt like they were destined to be a perpetual middle-of-the-standings team with Ball. They traded him in the hopes that getting worse now could make them championship contenders later.

Their fans probably could have lived with a small step back. What we've seen thus far has been a disaster. Not all of it is their fault. They've barely had Coby White or Kon Knueppel -- and Knueppel will be about another four weeks at least with a hamstring strain. Brandon Miller, the other cornerstone here who just signed a $209 million contract, is shooting 26% from 3 and below 36% from the floor because of how overburdened he currently is. A step back may have been the idea, but nobody thought it would be this bad, nor did many assume Ball would be this good for Minnesota. It doesn't change Charlotte's long-term outlook, but it makes the present that much more painful. All of the goodwill from last year's turnaround has seemingly evaporated.

We came into the season relatively certain about how the Western Conference was tiered. The Spurs and Thunder were at the top. The Lakers, the Wolves, the Houston Rockets and the Denver Nuggets would land between No. 3 and No. 6 in some order. After that? Well, no one gave much thought to the Play-In Tournament. The East was supposed to be the deep conference. That's an opinion we cycle through every four or five years. Every year is supposed to be the East's year, and then it isn't. When the Memphis Grizzlies and Portland Trail Blazers were lighting on the world on fire, it seemed as though the West's depth had triumphed yet again.

It still is, on balance. The Warriors and the Dallas Mavericks, for instance, are strongly exceeding expectations. But the early excitement over Memphis and Portland, at least, is starting to wane. The Grizzlies traded a six-game winning streak for a three-game losing streak. The Blazers walked into the hardest stretch of their schedule thus far, took a loss to the Lakers and then got smacked around by the Spurs. With two games against the Thunder coming, Portland is seemingly coming back down to Earth. For a moment there, the New Orleans Pelicans looked as though they were figuring some things out on a four-game winning streak, but back-to-back losses have them out of the Play-In picture, at least for now.

These teams are still better than we figured they'd be, and there's still a bit of wiggle room in the West. Denver, for instance, looks enormously vulnerable. But the Spurs have won eight in a row. The Thunder have righted the ship. The Lakers, Wolves and Rockets are all as good as we thought or better. For a moment there, it looked like we were due some surprises out West. For now, it seems as though order has mostly been restored.

It is still much, much too early to draw any meaningful conclusions about lottery reform, but an early topic thus far this season has been how bad the bottom of the league still is despite the removal of the tanking incentive. With almost three weeks in the books, there are seven teams with either one or two victories. Between those seven teams, there are only three total victories over teams above .500. The Kings beat the Mavericks ... without Kyrie Irving. The Orlando Magic beat the Toronto Raptors ... without Kawhi Leonard, and their victory over the New York Knicks at least came with Jalen Suggs in the lineup. If Suggs and Paolo Banchero were healthy, the Magic would likely not be in this class.

Essentially, when the worst teams are playing against the best ones at anything resembling full strength, they've been hopeless. Inevitably, a certain number of teams is just going to be bad whether or not they're trying to lose. In fact, given this year's specific outlook, it's not even clear how motivated any of these bottom-tier teams are to actually win. The relegation zone isn't a threat to the Milwaukee Bucks, Brooklyn Nets, Utah Jazz or Los Angeles Clippers because they don't actually control their own first-round picks. You could argue that being in the relegation zone would actually be advantageous to the Chicago Bulls in order to minimize their odds of getting a top-five pick in the bad 2027 draft, because doing so, in concert with their No. 4 pick in 2026, would lock them out of a top-five pick in the stronger 2028 class.

We might not see the sort of overt tanking we've gotten in years past, but the question here is whether or not that will actually matter. With so many of these teams having minimal incentives to win, will they still shut down key players midway through the season? Even if they don't, will attendance and television ratings be better for these teams down the stretch just because they're nominally trying? We're months away from even starting to get answers to these questions, but any notions that reform would create 30 competitive teams have been quickly dismissed. Even in October and November, some teams are already pretty tough to watch.

#2684. High School Football: Centennial’s passing QB helps push Cougars past Shakopee, into 6A semis

Senior quarterback Jack Wiste started games under Centennial earlier this season, until the Cougars went to a more run-heavy option in Wesley Kukkonen.

But Wiste keeps answering every time he's called upon. Such was the case late in the first half of Friday's Class 6A quarterfinal against Shakopee.

With just a minute remaining in the second quarter and Centennial facing a 3rd and 5 from the Shakopee 41 yard line, Wiste was inserted. He immediately hit Brett Pullman for a 10-yard strike to move the chains. Then Wiste found Nolan Larson for a five-yard gain.

Then Wiste went back to Pullman for a 13-yard connection.

After taking a sack, Wiste hit Larson again, this time for an 18-yard touchdown with 21 ticks remaining in the half to give Centennial a 7-0 lead en route to its 10-6 victory over Shakopee.

The Cougars will meet Champlin Park in the state semifinals at 7 p.m. Thursday at U.S. Bank Stadium. Centennial fell, 14-7, to the Rebels back in September.

Shakopee scored early in the fourth on Friday on a Blake Betton 6-yard touchdown run. But Shakopee's ensuing extra point try was blocked by Samson Skudlarek to maintain Centennial's one-point advantage.

Keegan Prigge snuck a 38-yard kick over the crossbar later in the quarter to rebuild Centennial's lead to 10-6.

Centennial's defense finished the job from there, effectively putting the game on ice with a 4th down sack on Shakopee's ensuing possession.

Monona Grove 30, New Richmond 7: New Richmond trailed its Division 2 state semifinal 17-0 at the half, but responded with a touchdown run from North Dakota State commit Austyn Wittek early in the third quarter to pull within 10.

New Richmond then stonewalled Monona Grove on 4th and goal from the 1 yard line on Monona Grove's ensuing drive, but couldn't find anything else offensively for the remainder of the night.

Rock Ridge 21, Glenwood City 15: Jack Main hit Brock Wood on a 4-yard scoring strike on 4th and goal with 5 minutes, 37 seconds to play to bring the Hilltoppers to within 21-15 in the fourth quarter of its Division 7 semifinal on Friday.

Glenwood City then got a defensive stop and had a chance to win the game in the closing minutes, but a pair of incomplete passes near midfield led to a turnover on downs with 80 seconds to play to end the Hilltoppers' season.

#2683. Devin Booker’s clutch scoring carries Suns amid starting lineup woes

As precious seconds ticked off the clock late in Thursday night's matchup between the Phoenix Suns and Charlotte Hornets, it was abundantly clear that Charlotte was attempting to intentionally foul Devin Booker. And Booker? He was ready and willing to accept that foul.

Unfortunately, head official Scott Foster apparently had his attention elsewhere, despite the action unfolding approximately five feet in front of him. Perhaps he was looking into the front row, spotted Steve Nash, and began reminiscing about the good old days when he and his fellow officials allowed opponents to assault the two-time MVP with little consequence. Maybe he noticed Brandon Rafi sitting courtside and started thinking about calling Rafi Rafi the next time he needs a lawyer. Whatever was occupying his attention, it certainly wasn't the intentional foul taking place directly in front of him.

Booker responded with that familiar piercing stare, the one we've seen countless times when he's wondering how an official could possibly miss something so obvious. But there was still a basketball game to finish, and with Sion James approaching to provide a double team, Booker decided to take matters into his own hands. He dribbled left, rose up, and buried a 28-footer that effectively sealed the victory for Phoenix.

No whistle? No problem. Sometimes the best response to questionable officiating is to make the officials irrelevant. And in that moment, Devin Booker did exactly that.

That moment encapsulated just how great Devin Booker has been to begin this season, with the exception of his three-point performance against Oklahoma City. For a team navigating a discombobulated, duplicative roster that is ultimately going to go as far as Booker can carry it, the Suns' franchise cornerstone has been delivering. Nowhere has that been more evident than in the clutch.

Booker scored nine points in clutch time against Charlotte, continuing an impressive stretch of late-game execution. Through four clutch appearances this season, he's shooting 66.7% from the field, 50% from beyond the arc, and has a +8 plus/minus. Those are encouraging numbers for a player whose late-game efficiency became a legitimate concern last season.

What impressed me most against the Hornets wasn't necessarily the scoring. It was his decision-making. Every time Charlotte attempted to throw a double team his way, Booker recognized what was happening and responded decisively and appropriately. On one possession, he drove away from the pressure, penetrated the defense, and kicked the ball to Jordan Goodwin in the left corner for an open three-point opportunity. Goodwin missed the shot, but the process was exactly what you wanted to see. On another possession, Booker beat the double team himself and converted. He wasn't forcing the issue. He was reading the defense, understanding what was available, and making the appropriate decision.

We are currently witnessing what can only be described as a Devin Booker heater. Over his last 7 games, he's averaging 27.4 points on 49/40/95 splits.

Quite honestly, the Suns desperately need it because the rest of the starting lineup is struggling mightily. Perhaps it's the lack of continuity and limited playing time together. Maybe it's the absence of clearly defined roles, with players still attempting to understand where they fit within an offense that features overlapping skill sets. Whatever the explanation, the production from Phoenix's starters has been inconsistent and inefficient.

Booker has accounted for 35.1% of all points scored by the Suns' starting lineup this season. Think about that. More than one out of every three points produced by the starters has come from a single player. Meanwhile, the starters not named Devin Booker have combined to shoot 52-of-154 from beyond the arc, a pedestrian 33.8%. In the clutch, everyone without 'Booker' written on their back has combined to make 20% of their threes and 30% of their shots.

While the shooting inefficiencies that plagued Booker last season generated plenty of concern, those issues haven't carried over into the early portion of this campaign. Against Charlotte, he connected on 4-of-8 attempts from deep, continuing to provide the offensive production and efficiency that Phoenix needs from its best player. He's up to 25.5 points this season, doing so on 50/38/94 splits, adding 5.0 assists, and 1.2 steals.

Until the rest of the starting five figures out who they are, what their responsibilities should be, and how they can contribute more effectively on both ends of the floor, the Suns are going to need Booker to keep this heater going. Because if he has an ordinary night, there's a pretty good chance Phoenix is going to lose. That's an unfortunate reality, but it's where this organization finds itself.

Devin Booker is in the prime of his career. This should be the period when the franchise has a clear understanding of what works alongside him, what complements his strengths, and how to construct a roster that maximizes his abilities. The organization has had plenty of time to figure that out.

Instead, we've watched Phoenix spend much of his prime fumbling through roster construction, repeatedly acquiring players with overlapping skill sets and similar positional responsibilities. Rather than consistently surrounding Booker with complementary pieces, the organization has continued placing additional weight on his shoulders, asking him to compensate for deficiencies that should have been addressed through better roster construction. Thankfully, at least through the opening weeks of this season, Booker appears more than willing to accept that responsibility.

But how long can he sustain it? How long can a team reasonably expect one player to account for more than a third of its starting lineup's scoring while simultaneously serving as its primary offensive organizer and late-game closer? At some point, the supporting cast has to establish its identity and begin providing consistent production.

I've been quick to remind people that Devin Booker is the $57 million man whenever his performances fall short of expectations. When you're earning that kind of money, there's a certain level of production, leadership, and accountability that comes with the paycheck. And right now? He's earning every damn dollar.

You earn that money by delivering in the clutch, which Booker has done. You earn it by becoming the stabilizing force that prevents an inconsistent team from completely unraveling. Check that too, as the team sits at 5-6. You earn it by showing up night after night, accepting the responsibility of carrying an offense while your teammates are still trying to figure out their roles, their responsibilities, and perhaps why they're being asked to occupy spaces already filled by somebody else. That's what Devin Booker has been doing.

And while I certainly hope the rest of the roster begins providing him with the support he deserves, there's something worth appreciating about watching a player embrace that burden and continue delivering. Because for all the questions surrounding the Phoenix Suns right now, Devin Booker is providing the most important answer. He's playing like the $57 million man.

We've spent plenty of time questioning Booker's late-game execution, his decision-making, and whether he can consistently elevate a flawed roster. Right now, he's answering those questions with his play. The Suns still have plenty to figure out, and Booker can't be expected to carry them indefinitely. But for the moment, he's reminding everyone why he's the face of this franchise. And why, when the game is on the line, you probably shouldn't leave him open from 28 feet.

#2682. Remembering a Random Packers Game: The Minnesota Vikings

The last time I wrote about a random game between the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, I covered a 1999 matchup the Packers had won. The 2026 Packers proceeded to lose in spectacular fashion to open the season, and I think it's because I jinxed them. Following that same logic, I'm using my voodoo magic to conjure up a win for Week 10. This week's random Packers vs. Vikings game is the 90th meeting between the two teams, when the Packers lost 20-17 on November 21st, 2005.

The 2005 Packers were…pretty bad! They lost WR Javon Walker to a torn ACL in Week 1, and both RBs Ahman Green and Najeh Davenport were placed on IR with leg injuries. With a 2-7 record coming into their matchup against the 4-5 Vikings, the Packers had turned the ball over 20 times already. This was a far cry from the team who had won the NFC North at 10-6 the previous year while having two WRs with 1,200+ yards (Javon Walker and Donald Driver) AND a 1,100 yard rusher (Ahman Green). The team had already lost to Minnesota by 3 points in Week 7—it was time to right the ship.

On the Vikings' side, they had recently lost starting QB Daunte Culpepper to a catastrophic knee injury. Taking his place was veteran Brad Johnson, who had the Vikings on a bit of a hot streak after two straight wins. Losing Culpepper certainly wasn't ideal, but the Vikings were finding ways to win.

After a missed 49-yard field goal attempt by the Vikings on their opening drive, QB Brett Favre and the Packers offense responded by going 3 and out. The Vikings offense proceeded to do exactly the same thing. The first score of the game came on the Packers' next drive after a couple of big plays, including a 30 yard pass to RB Samkon Gado, and then a 15 yard pass to WR Donald Driver in the endzone.

The Vikings' next drive ended with an interception by S Nick Collins. Things were looking up for the Packers! Just kidding. Both offenses proceeded to combine for 6 straight punts. Favre then decided enough was enough—someone needed to score! So he threw a 51 yard pick-six to CB Dovonte Edwards.

With about 30 seconds left in the 2nd quarter, the gunslinger rattled off a 53-yard yard pass to Donald Driver, and the Packers found themselves with a 14-7 lead at halftime.

After more unsavory play by both offenses, the Vikings tied it up 14-14 in the 3rd quarter after RB Ciatrick Fason rushed for a 1 yard TD, capping off a nearly 9 minute drive. This would be the final touchdown scored by either team. The teams proceeded to trade punts and field goals, and with 3 seconds left, Vikings K Paul Edinger nailed the 27 yard dagger. Packers lose, 20-17.

Brett Favre finished the day 20 of 33 for 227 yards, 2 TDs, and 2 INTs. Tony Fisher led the team on the ground, finishing with a whopping 14 yards on 4 carries, while Donald Driver finished with 5 catches on 9 targets for 84 yards and 2 TDs.

All the big moments from this game can be found here.

The Packers fell to 2-8 on the season, and would go on to win just 2 more games all year, finishing 4-12 for the team's first losing record since 1991 (also 4-12). The 2005 Packers turned the ball over 45 times, while scoring just 31 TDs on offense. HC Mike Sherman was fired less than a year after receiving a contract extension, and the team replaced him with Another Mike™, Mike McCarthy. Their 4-12 record earned them the 5th overall pick in the 2006 NFL Draft, which they used to select LB A.J. Hawk.

The Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings will meet for the 133rd time on Sunday, during the day's early slate of games at 1pm ET/12pm CT.

#2680. NBA Cup 2026: Knicks drop to last place in group play with loss to shorthanded Pacers, Spurs dominate Warriors

The 2025-26 season was a dream for the New York Knicks, from the NBA Cup to the NBA Finals. This season is shaping up differently.

The defending Cup champions fell to 0-2 in group play on Friday with a 106-104 loss to the Indiana Pacers, who are still playing without Tyrese Haliburton due to a left hamstring strain. That puts New York in the bottom of the East Group B standings and all but eliminates them from the in-season tournament.

No team with two losses in group play has reached the knockout rounds in the NBA Cup since its introduction in 2023.

Beyond the NBA Cup, the loss dropped the Knicks to 6-6 in the regular season, continuing a slow start for a team that brought back nearly every contributor from last year's champion.

The game was nearly another epic comeback for the Knicks, who were down by 14 late in the third quarter but had the game tied early in the fourth. The Pacers responded with a 13-2 run to reassert control and held off one last Knicks push in the final minute.

New York cut an eight-point lead to two in the final two minutes and had a chance to steal the win when an inbounds pass went wrong for the Pacers (not helped by a missed foul call by the refs), but Karl-Anthony Towns' would-be game-tying shot clanked away.

Every Pacers starter scored in double figures, with Pascal Siakam leading the team with 19 points. That plus 29 bench points was enough to counter a 33-point, 11-assist night by Jalen Brunson.

Let's just say the second marquee game of the night did not come down to the final possession.

A clash of Western Conference contenders saw the San Antonio Spurs score the first 18 points of the game against the Golden State Warriors, who are still playing without Stephen Curry.

It honestly didn't get much better from there. The Spurs were up 63-33 at halftime and led by as much as 43 during a 123-85 blowout. That game-opening run broke a Spurs franchise record.

Stephon Castle led the Spurs with 32 points on 12-of-18 shooting, while Victor Wembanyama contributed 12 points, 12 rebounds, 6 assists and 2 blocks. The win gives the Spurs a commanding lead in West Group C.

#2679. A Realistic View of What Kirk Cousins 2.0 Brings to the Vikings

The Minnesota Vikings made the move they had to make after a half-season of underwhelming quarterback performance in trading for Kirk Cousins. He will be the starter as soon as possible, which is likely to be this Sunday against the Packers. His arrival has come with much fanfare as the savior of the Vikings offense who, combined with the Vikings dominant defense and good special teams, could position the Vikings for a deep run in the post-season.

But a quarterback switching teams in mid-season is not without its difficulties, even with Cousins' familiarity with Kevin O'Connell's scheme and some of the key players around him from Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson to Brian O'Neill, Blake Brandel, and Christian Darrisaw. It's also an advantage that Cousins has been playing the entire season, so he doesn't have to get acclimated to playing again, as a backup quarterback who hasn't played would need to do.

If Cousins plays on Sunday (as expected at this point), there could be some hiccups as he works out timing and other rapport issues in his first game back after three years. But Cousins has been playing in the same type of offense under Klint Kubiak in Las Vegas, and is probably the most well-versed quarterback in Kevin O'Connell's scheme in the league- and one of the most well-suited to execute it.

The first graphic compares Cousins' rate and EPA efficiency in the play-action passing game, which is central to KOC's offense. He's been one of the more effective quarterbacks out of play-action for most of his career, and has run it at a relatively high rate for most of his 15-year career. He's also played at a relatively high rate from under center, which KOC also likes to do to make the play-action game more effective. Cousins' career passer rating from under center is 107.2, and in play-action it is 110.0. This season, Cousins' passer rating with play-action is 123.4.

The Vikings have used play-action more than the Raiders have so far this season. Part of that is game situation- both down-and-distance and score/time remaining. You would think that with the Vikings dominant defense, they would continue to be able to run play action at a high rate to maximize Cousins' strength in that area.

The second graphic represents Cousins' passing metrics to each part of the field. The big takeaway is that the lion's share of Cousins' passing yards and attempts are between the numbers. He's also had good success throwing at intermediate depth (10-19 yards) this season. That's another important element of KOC's scheme-targeting the middle of the field. Both Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz have been reluctant to target the middle of the field, which compromises the effectiveness of O'Connell's scheme. One of the staples of O'Connell's scheme is the dagger route combination, which has largely disappeared from run or targeted routes this season. It's also one of the most effective route combinations for Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison.

Bottom line, having Kirk Cousins at quarterback should open up the entirety of KOC's playbook, but it may take some time for Cousins to re-familiarize himself with the playbook and get on the same page again with receivers. Still, I don't anticipate Cousins hesitating to get the ball out to open receivers as Murray and Wentz have done this season.

Since the last time Cousins played for the Vikings- three years ago- he had his Achilles tendon repaired and spent most of his time in Atlanta recovering from that. At that point it looked like he was done. His passes lacked velocity and his movement was slower than it had been. Apparently, he couldn't really push off of his foot with the repaired Achilles and that was negatively affecting his game. But after signing with the Raiders, it appears that Cousins has fully recovered from the Achilles injury and no longer has the issues that plagued him in Atlanta. The velocity is back and while Cousins has never been particularly mobile, he is able to move like he used to before the Achilles injury. According to Albert Breer, when the Vikings were looking into trading for Cousins, after, "meshing the scouts' and coaches' analysis, they saw Cousins as still possessing a live arm and deadly accuracy and having returned to the baseline of athleticism he set before tearing his Achilles in 2024, evidenced on tape in the keeper game that's essential to Kubiak's scheme."

I've watched all of Cousins' throws with the Raiders this year, and it is reminiscent of his previous stint with the Vikings. I don't know that his arm strength has declined much- it doesn't look like it- but there is a caveat. He can make all the throws, as you would expect from a starting NFL quarterback, but he needs to step-in to deeper throws for them to have the needed velocity. That may have been the case before as well but it is something that stood out when watching his tape this season. He can't launch balls down field with velocity off his back foot like Jordan Love or Caleb Williams. This is the impact of being his being 38 years old. Additionally, he has not become any more mobile over the last three years, and the scampering of Kyler Murray to pick up first downs here and there is definitely not in Cousins' bag, if that wasn't obvious. He has run for five-yard gains on a couple occasions this season, but that's about it. He is able to maneuver within the pocket effectively and does fine on bootlegs, but he's not going to outrun many pass rushers for very long. He's also not afraid to deliver the ball downfield in the face of oncoming pressure- and pay the price for it. He's also not afraid of throwing into tight windows and does so with regularity.

Cousins has 8 interceptions so far this season, three of which came last weekend against the 49ers. A few of them came on throws left a bit short, a few in tight window throws where ball placement and/or route were not ideal. One his receiver fell down. And the last one came with 4 minutes left in the 49ers game and he was just trying make something happen down multiple scores. But for the most part Cousins' interceptions came while being aggressive and playing on time making throws that Murray and Wentz have generally avoided this season.

Cousins hasn't been sacked much so far this season- just 11 times in 9 games. He's also the only quarterback who has not been sacked on a blitz so far this season. So, he's generally done an excellent job of avoiding the rush and getting the ball out- maybe only one of sacks can be blamed on him. And whereas Murray or Wentz may look to scramble to buy time, Cousins is mainly focused on getting the ball out. He's very much a pocket passer in that respect, with his only move typically being to step up in the pocket to avoid the edge rush.

The Raiders offense has different strengths than the Vikings, and that has influenced Cousins' play. Their offensive line is similar strength as the Vikings, anchored by All-Pro center Tyler Linderbaum. But the strength of their receiver group is their tight ends- Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer- and they run double tight-end sets at the highest rate in the league. Their receivers are Tre Tucker and former Viking Jalen Nailor. The Raiders running game is terrible- last in the league- averaging just 2.9 yards per carry. Ashton Jeanty hasn't done much as a running back, but he is a good receiving back. So, roughly 60% of Cousins' targets with the Raiders were to tight ends or running backs- mainly Jeanty.

Cousins has the third highest PFF passing grade (91.6) when targeting intermediate (10-19 yard) routes this season among starting quarterbacks and has done so at the fifth-highest rate (24.8%). Most of those targets were to tight ends between the numbers. Cousins is likely to target wide receivers more with the Vikings- as he did in 2022-23- as that is the strength of the Vikings receiver group. But the route concepts the Vikings employ will likely have him continue to target intermediate routes over the middle at a fairly high clip, complemented by outside zone runs that can spread the defense out and make linebackers bite on play action.

In addition to having a poor running game, the Raiders also have the last ranked defense in both points and yards allowed. They've allowed at least 30 points in each of their last six games, which has put Cousins under pressure to keep pace. That has affected the game situation and play calling for the Raiders, which pass just over 60% of the time- one of the higher rates in the league.

Still, despite a poor supporting cast when it comes to the running game and defense, Cousins has managed a top ten ranking (7th) across a composite of key quarterback metrics this season. That's leaps and bounds higher than anything the Vikings have had so far this season.

By most metrics, Cousins' performance this season has been pretty close to his season average across five and a half seasons with the Vikings previously, so from an age standpoint there doesn't seem to be an impediment there to his achieving similar results with the Vikings this season compared to what he did with the Raiders and compared to what he did previously in Minnesota. The schemes in Las Vegas and Minnesota are similar- both from the Shanahan tree- and Cousins' spent a year and a half in O'Connell's system already and three and a half seasons with Justin Jefferson, a half season with Jordan Addison and a year and a half with T.J. Hockenson. It's really a question of how fast everything comes back to him. It wouldn't be surprising if there is a ramp up period, but from all accounts he's hit the ground running since he arrived on Tuesday. My guess is there will be hiccups on Sunday as he gets back into the swing of the Vikings offense- and maybe here and there for a few games- but I also expect him to make more throws than we've been seeing from Murray and Wentz this season. Whether that's enough to beat the Packers and 49ers remains to be seen, and once again the Vikings' defense will need to show up and be dominant, but Cousins should be able to allow the Vikings offense to possess the ball and put them in position to score more points than they have so far this season- even with a more limited playbook and kind of re-learning on the field as far as rapport with receivers.

How quickly Cousins can get up to speed with the Vikings offense could mean the difference between a division championship and potential first seed in the playoffs and a wild card spot, assuming the Vikings beat the weaker teams remaining on their schedule. But the next two games are crucial- the Packers and 49ers- in terms of keeping pace within the division and competing for the top seed in the postseason. If the Vikings can win them both, they move to 8-2 and have a much easier schedule the rest of the season and would hold a key tie-breaker against the 49ers. If they lose both games, they fall to 6-4 and if they can regroup from there to gain a wild card spot they will play on the road throughout the playoffs in all likelihood. That's a tough road to make a deep run. But if the Vikings and Cousins ramp up to play their best football in December- and beyond- they will be as formidable a team as there is in the league and not a team any division winner is looking forward to playing.

But a premium is on winning in November- beginning on Sunday- to best position the team for a deep run. Hopefully Cousins- and the rest of the team- is up to the task.

#2678. Lafayette Jeff football's postseason ends in regional with loss to Warsaw

LAFAYETTE — Jeff football lined up together on its side of the field, as it does every week, but it wasn't in the same way its grown accustomed to over the last several weeks.

The Bronchos made history with their third consecutive sectional championship this season, but the road ended at the regional once again with a 49-39 loss to Warsaw on Friday, Nov. 13. On the other side of the field, the Tigers celebrated their second regional title with the trophy raised in the air.

Coach Pat Shanley acknowledged it was one that hurt. He called senior leader Ka'vion Campbell-Walker up to make a departing speech, who commanded every player's attention with a passionate message to the underclassmen to carry on the work when he's gone.

More: Lafayette area IHSAA football regional championship game scores, updates

More: Benton Central's Claire Whaley voted Nov. 2-8 J&C Athlete of the Week, sponsored by Ivy Tech

He and other seniors, such as wide receiver Bryce VanOstran, quarterback Trysten Barrett and defensive lineman Chris Hardy, have laid the foundation for the program over the years. That group has helped them get to a place where they can be surefire sectional winners each season and have chances to make it deeper into November.

The Bronchos couldn't quite kick down the doors of regional this year. But they have no doubts that they'll continue to build the foundation up and accomplish that soon.

"We have a program that is only going to continue to get better," Shanley said. "We have people in this community that are really committed and understand what we're doing and what we're building. You have kids that really believe in it and they love it. … We're going to fight, claw and scratch to find ways to get better and to kick that door in.

On the opening drive, VanOstran got the crowd at Schuemann Stadium fired up with a 63-yard touchdown at the 10:01 mark of the first quarter off a pass from Barrett. It was a whole lot of yards after the catch, and VanOstran skipped his way to celebrate the moment in front of the crowd. That was the energy Jeff needed to start the night.

But Warsaw's flexbone triple option offense, a style of play that Jeff has grown to be familiar with over the years, quickly took over. The Tigers tied it up at 7-7 at the 5:11 mark, but their next drive signaled something that the Broncho defense couldn't contain for the rest of the game.

Quarterback Mark Haynes broke loose and went untouched for an 80-yard touchdown with 1:27 remaining in the first, before converting a two-point conversion to give Warsaw a 15-10 lead. The defensive breakdowns happened again at the 3:22 mark in the second, in which Brady Sauer bounced to the outside and down the sideline for a 50-yard touchdown on fourth-and-2.

By the end of the first half, the Tigers led 29-10.

"You got to stop a quarterback/fullback, right? So, you're kind of damned if you do and damned if you don't," Shanley said of the Warsaw run game. "We spent a lot of time studying it. … (coach Bart Curtis) is a Hall of Famer. He runs that flexbone as well as anybody in the country. He's a really, really good coach."

Warsaw switched it up to start the second half. It opted for a pass play, in which lineman Grady Nelson snuck by the Jeff defense for a wide-open catch to score a 46-yard passing touchdown at the 9:11 mark of the third quarter.

The Bronchos needed to score quickly, which they found a rhythm in throughout the second half. Barrett threw another shot for an explosive play at the 8:11 mark in which receiver Na'Darius Young caught it and raced down the sideline for a 66-yard touchdown on third-and-11.

Both VanOstran and Young finished the night with another touchdown each, the latter of which followed a fumble recovery from linebacker Myles Stetler. But Warsaw kept battling back on the ground to prevent a big enough dent in its lead, including a 48-yard touchdown from Ethan Rivich with 11:33 remaining in the fourth to go up 49-24.

"They got some stops on us in the second quarter, and unfortunately, we couldn't get enough stops to get on the right side of the scoreboard," Shanley said.

Although disappointment was felt on the field in the aftermath of the loss, a lot of optimism remained. Jeff won't sit this one for too long; the mindset is already on next season.

There will be new talent added to the fold and players that have to step into bigger roles. But as the Bronchos find a way to do each year, they plan to do it again. There's a lot of work to be done, but that's just part of the process.

"There's so many good kids that are coming back," Shanley said. "The foundation's laid. Again, it's just going to boil down to the work that we do in the offseason. We got to grow, we got to get bigger. … I know we got the right people on the bus."

Chase Gemes covers high school sports and Purdue women's basketball for the Journal & Courier. He can be reached at cgemes@usatodayco.com.

#2675. Rapid Recap: Magic 107, Bucks 99

The Milwaukee Bucks fall to 0/2 in the NBA Cup and 1-12 overall, losing to the Orlando Magic 107-99 in a game that was at least competitive. Jaime Jaquez Jr. led the Bucks yet again with 22 points off the bench on 8/15 shooting and 5/7 from three. Franz Wagner starred for the Magic, dropping a near triple-double of 35 points, 12 assists, and nine rebounds (at one point it was a triple-double, but they apparently retracted a rebound).

With Ousmane Dieng getting the surprise start, the Bucks began slowly, with Myles Turner turning the ball over twice in the first two possessions and the team going 1/5 from the field and 1/4 from the charity stripe as the Magic led 12-4 at the seven-minute mark. Milwaukee responded, however, with a 10-3 run, thanks in large part to Kel'el Ware, who impacted early with a put-back slam and a corner triple. We even got treated to first-quarter Gary Trent Jr. minutes, but his elite defence couldn't stop Franz Wagner, who carved up the visitors in the pick-and-roll as the Magic took a 23-15 lead into the first major break.

Wagner continued to kill the Bucks early in the second, nailing two threes to extend Orlando's lead to 13 just over two minutes in as Milwaukee's shooting woes continued. Thankfully, a select few Bucks were shooting well, including Myles Turner, who nailed his third three of the night to cut the deficit to 10 with seven minutes to play. After starting 0/5, Tyler Herro began to cook as the second wore on, hitting a three, a floater, and a few free throws as the Bucks inched closer, down 34-28 halfway through the period. Unfortunately, the Magic closed on an 18-8 run as their balanced attack dominated the Bucks on both ends, leading 52-36 at the half.

Coach Jenkins started Nate Ament in Dieng's place to start the third, and the rookie paid that faith off, opening the quarter with a corner three after going 1/6 in the first half. In general, the Bucks looked much more fluid on offence, but they couldn't get stops as Desmond Bane punished them twice from deep to give his side a 65-45 edge four minutes in. The visitors wouldn't give in, though; they knuckled down on defence, which allowed them to play more in transition and go on a 10-0 run. That said, the Bucks had major free throw issues, making just 7/15 (!) midway through the third. That's when Bane really started to cook, knocking in a three plus the foul, then another three on the next possession as the margin blew back out to 16. Jaime Jaquez Jr. was huge to close the quarter, though, nailing multiple bombs and a mid-range shot to keep the Bucks within shouting distance, down 84-72 after three.

It was a frantic start to the fourth, with Milwaukee giving up plenty of open looks but the Magic failing to hit any; as a result, the visitors kept their deficit around 10 as they lived at the line. The Magic's lead stayed around that margin for the next four minutes as the Bucks' parade to the charity stripe continued (though they kept missing when they got there). In fact, Milwaukee didn't hit a field goal for over six minutes, but remarkably, they remained (somewhat) in the game. In the end, though, Wagner was too much, leading his side to their first home victory of the season.

The Bucks were atrocious from the free throw line, making just 18 of 31 attempts in a game they lost by eight. Kyle Kuzma shot a staggering 7/15 on his own!

I physically cannot watch Kuzma-ball anymore, man. It's buyout time (even though I get that he has no incentive to want that).

#2674. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.
