#2673. Bloom-Carroll volleyball title hopes fall short in state semifinal

VANDALIA — During its tournament run to the state volleyball tournament, the Bloom-Carroll volleyball team was always able to overcome some early pitfalls, and during their Division III state semifinal against Padua Franciscan, it looked as if the Bulldogs were going to follow the same script.

The Bears won the first set, but Bloom-Carroll came right back to tie it up in the second. In the all-important third set, the Bulldogs could not get over the hump and lost a heartbreaker.

The Bulldogs were not able to overcome that, and the Bears were able to finish them off in the fourth set and post a 25-22, 22-25, 28-26, 25-14 victory on Friday night, Nov. 13, at Vandalia-Butler High School.

More: 'We want to win it all' | Bloom Carroll eyes state title

Even though the Bulldogs fought back, they made some uncharacteristic mistakes, and in the end, it cost them.

"We struggled, especially in that fourth set, and I think it's one of those things where you really don't want to think it could come to an end," Bloom-Carroll coach Kyle McFerin said. "I thought we made winning plays in the third set, and we played to win, but we couldn't get the win, and then we came out flat in the fourth set. We just couldn't get it going. We kind of got in our own way at times, with more net calls than we usually get, and we hit a few more balls out-of-bounds than we usually do. This is a state semifinal game, and you can't do those things and expect to win."

The third set was crucial and could have gone either way. Each time the Bulldogs were forced to score, they did, but they could never take the lead down the stretch and eventually fell.

"We were right there in the fourth set, but they were able to make a few more plays," McFerin said. "If we win that, who knows how things would have turned out."

Alya Mitchell had a solid game and led the Bulldogs with 15 kills. Renee Smith had 30 assists, and Kylynne Solberger had 19 digs. Josie Burr chipped in eight kills, Kylee Reiser finished with five kills, 10 digs and five aces, and Maddie Fox added seven kills.

Bloom-Carroll, which went undefeated in the Mid-State League-Buckeye Division, finishes with a 22-5 overall record. The Bulldogs were state runner-up in 2025 and made back-to-back state tournament appearances for the first time in school history. Over the last two years, they have won 49 games.

Bloom-Carroll's five seniors have helped raise the bar for the program.

"It is hard right now, but the five seniors we had were great this year," McFerin said. "This was a challenging season in a lot of ways, but they responded, and we grew together. We weren't a team at the beginning of the season, and we became a team as the season went on, and that's hard to do. They did a great job of progressing, and that's a credit to them. They have been to two straight final fours, and they have done a great job moving the program forward."

#2672. Giannis Antetokounmpo stunned by Doc Rivers' 'bitterness and pettiness' after former coach's criticism

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Miami Heat have gotten off to a slow start to Giannis Antetokounmpo's first season in south Florida, which has led to plenty of discussion about Antetokounmpo's fit with Bam Adebayo and the challenges of building around Giannis.

Among those to chime in on the topic is Antetokounmpo's former coach, Doc Rivers, who struggled to get the most out of the star in Milwaukee and never got Antetokounmpo and Damian Lillard on the same page. Rivers recently offered some critiques of Antetokounmpo, noting he's a difficult star to coach because of his play style and a defiance about changing how he plays.

On Sunday, after the Heat beat the Kings, Antetokounmpo was taken aback when asked about the comments by his former coach.

"You have his number, right? You do. I know you do. You gotta go ask him why he thought that; that's on him," Antetokounmpo told The Athletic. "That's not on me. I gotta focus on my team and what I gotta do and how can I be better and how can I help the team. But like, goddamn. That's crazy. Never let bitterness and pettiness get in front of your goals and dreams, man. For every athlete out there, never let that [happen]. That's insane, but you gotta go ask him why he said what he said. Not me."

Rivers' tenure in Milwaukee was a disaster: he took over for Adrian Griffin in the middle of the 2023-24 season with the Bucks 30-13 and proceeded to go 97-103 in his three years with the Bucks. Given Rivers' history of shifting blame, Antetokounmpo can more easily brush aside his critique as Doc once again finding someone else to blame for his team's shortcomings.

However, while Rivers might not be an infallible messenger, he did have some interesting comments about the challenge of coaching Antetokounmpo this week on The Bill Simmons Podcast.

"He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have super IQ at the same time," Rivers said. "It's really a strange thing. And he really has one way. Downhill, forceful. Every play, he wants to force it.

"There's times where I wish he'd do one thing. I wish he'd learn how to execute better," Rivers added. "He's one of those guys, you get a lot of them from the U.S., AAU guys, who have never needed to execute, because they can do it on their own. That doesn't help the team."

It's not surprising that Antetokounmpo would balk at those comments, but viewing from the outside, there certainly seems to be validity to at least some of what Rivers says. Questioning a player's IQ will always understandably irk them, but watching Antetokounmpo play with Lillard and now Adebayo, the criticism of him wanting to attack downhill and not adjusting his play style has been apparent for some time.

What might help the Heat the most here is that, for as stubborn as Antetokounmpo can be, he is also fueled by a desire to prove people wrong. While Rivers may have been unable to get Antetokounmpo to buy into changing his style while playing for him, criticizing the former MVP might lead Giannis to show he can adapt his style purely out of spite.

#2670. Steelers could be forced to bus to Cincinnati after FAA grounds flights

The Pittsburgh Steelers are set to take on the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday Night Football for sole possession of first place in the AFC North. However, travel plans could have to change drastically for the Steelers over the course of the next 24 hours.

Just a few hours ago, the FAA grounded all flights nationwide after what they are calling a communications problem. At the time of this writing, Homeland Security does not believe that this was a nefarious attack against the U.S., but rather just an outage. This is the first nationwide ground stoppage since January 2023.

Steelers senior director of communications Burt Lauten told WPXI's Shelby Cassesse that the team is "monitoring the situation" as air travel comes to a halt.

It's difficult to say how long this ground stoppage could last, and it could effect sporting events all across the nation throughout the weekend. Luckily for the Steelers, the drive to Cincinnati would be something they could quickly pivot to.

Since the team was not scheduled to fly out until Saturday, they are in a better situation than most right now. While a flight is quicker and more convenient for the team, a bus ride shouldn't have a major effect on their preparation plans, as it may for other teams.

#2668. How Paul George is fittingly in perfectly (very) early in his Celtics tenure

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Paul George has been in the NBA since 2011. He's made nine All-Star appearances, six All-NBA Teams and four All-Defensive Teams, and scored nearly 20,000 points. But he knew that he would have to prove himself all over again in Boston after he arrived this summer in a blockbuster trade that sent Celtics icon and fan favorite Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers.

"I understand my circumstances. I understand how huge JB was, not only for the organization, but here in the city. So, I didn't take it personal," George said at his introductory press conference, regarding the negative reaction to the trade. "To be honest, they should have a relationship, emotionally, to that trade. But my job is to kind of come into a great opportunity for me."

"It's a new group, a new opportunity," George continued. "I think they're getting someone that's ready to -- not fill the shoes or fill the void of JB -- but I think from a personal standpoint myself, I think I can come in and kind of still keep us in that contention. Give us a chance to win."

It's taken George just a few weeks to earn the trust of Celtics fans and show that he can still contribute to winning.

After pouring in 27 points in a 20-point win over the Milwaukee Bucks on Sunday, George is averaging 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and a career-high 2.3 steals, while shooting a career-high 42.5% from 3-point range for the 8-2 Celtics, who sit in second place in the Eastern Conference behind the 9-2 Sixers.

Those old rivals will meet Tuesday in a highly anticipated showdown that will be Brown and George's first games against their old teams.

"It'll be great to see those guys and compete against them finally," George said Sunday. "Obviously, Philly was a special place for me. It was a rough, you know, tenure, my two years there, but it'll be special to be in the building."

Ahead of George's return to Philadelphia, let's take a closer look at how he's shined so far in Boston:

"We have a superstar and that's [Jayson Tatum]," George said during his introductory press conference. "I'm not here to steal the shine or reinvent who I am. I'm here to help JT. He's the guy."

As great as Tatum and Brown were together, there was always some underlying tension over their place in the organization. Brown, who was named Eastern Conference Finals MVP and Finals MVP in 2024 when the Celtics won the title, saw himself as Tatum's equal. That was especially true after Brown led the Celtics to 56 wins last season while Tatum missed the majority of the campaign rehabbing from a torn Achilles.

Trading Brown for George established a clear hierarchy in the locker room. The Celtics are Tatum's team, and George is happy to play a supporting role. Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla praised George for being "very coachable, very open-minded" and setting a "very high" standard.

"The way we're asking him to play is maybe a little bit different than what he's been asked to do in the past. He enjoys that, he's open-minded to it and he just works at it. He's very hard on himself. Holds himself to a very high standard, constantly watching film, taking notes in his journal and just processing the game. He takes pride in learning and getting better and you're seeing the fruits of that," Mazzulla said Sunday.

George has always been a high-level 3-point shooter, but he's spent most of his career having to create looks for himself. In Boston, playing alongside Tatum in a system that prioritizes shooting and spacing, George has thrived as a high-volume catch-and-shoot threat.

He's shooting 46% on 5.6 catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game -- both marks are career-highs. George is tied for 10th in the league in catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game, and among the 16 players taking at least five such attempts, he's tied for second in percentage, behind only Steph Curry (54.9%).

Most efficient high-volume catch-and-shoot threats in 2026-27

By comparison, Brown has never shot 40% from 3-point range for a season in his career, and hasn't even shot above 40% on catch-and-shoot attempts since 2021. George's willingness to accept more of an off-ball role, and ability to knock down those shots at an extremely high rate, is a big reason why he's fit in so seamlessly in Boston.

George's five 3s against the Bucks on Sunday were all of the catch-and-shoot variety.

"Watching him shoot like that is unbelievable," Celtics big man Mitchell Robinson said Sunday. "Played against him quite a few times and to be on the same side of the ball with him and cheer him on instead of boo[ing him], it's great."

Overall, George is shooting 42.5% on a team-high 8.1 3-point attempts per game. His hot shooting is a big reason why the Celtics are sixth in the league in 3-point percentage (37.6%) even though Tatum (31.3%) and Derrick White (32.7%) have been ice cold to start the season.

George hasn't made an All-Defensive Team since 2019, when he finished third in Defensive Player of the Year voting with the Oklahoma City Thunder, in large part due to injuries. He remains an elite team defender, though, and will get back to the All-Defensive level this season if he stays healthy and keeps defending like he has through the first 10 games.

When asked about George on Sunday, Tatum singled out his new teammate's "super-high IQ" and "incredible defensive instincts."

George has been particularly impressive off the ball this season. He's wreaking havoc in the passing lanes with his length, timing and anticipation. George's 2.3 steals are a career-high and good for fourth in the league, and he's third in deflections per game with 5.1. Of the four players averaging at least five deflections per game, he is by far the oldest at 36.

George's effort is a big reason why the Celtics are forcing way more turnovers than they ever have under Mazzulla. Their opponent turnover rate is 17.4%, which ranks sixth in the league; in Mazzulla's first four seasons in charge, the Celtics never had an opponent turnover rate above 13.1% and never finished higher than 24th in the league in that category.

#2666. Xavier 81-63 Mississippi State: Recap

Winning all the buy games in the world by 45 is nice, but it isn't going to move the needle in March when it comes time to evaluate a team's resume for the NCAA Tournament. To get there, you have to beat someone with substance at some point and Xavier took their first chance to do so with style tonight at The Greenbrier. Mississippi State is not expected to challenge at the top of the SEC this season, but they are a solid Q2 opportunity on a neutral floor and the first line on a resume Xavier hopes to fill out before Selection Sunday.

The Bulldogs grabbed the first four points of the night, but Xavier punched back immediately and never gave the lead back after Tru Washington (21/8/4) put on a personal 5-0 run. Washington was Xavier's star tonight, but he was far from alone in putting his stamp on the first half as Nikos Chitikoudis (11/6/1) stepped into the void left by Mike Nwoko's (4/6/1) foul issues and gave Xavier 12 excellent minutes in the first frame. Xavier started to gain separation near the midway point of the half when Ruben Dominguez (9/0/0) was fouled shooting a three and cashed out all three free throws then cut out the middle man and drained a three the next time down to put X up 7 and put the Bulldogs on the ropes. Mississippi State star Josh Hubbard sparked to life to bring the game back to within a point with 3:34 to play, but Xavier grabbed back the momentum through back to back threes from Kalek House (3/4/3) and Gabriel Pozzato (9/1/0) and, after a bit of back and forth, a four point play from Pozzato stake Xavier to a 10 point halftime lead and gave this team a chance to show they had learned from last year's heartbreaks and could close out a contest.

In a series of events familiar to people who remembered the first half of the game, Mississippi State scored first and then Tru Washington scored Xavier's first five points followed by a Nikos Chitikoudis bucket. That pushed the lead to a dozen and a triple from Jovan Milicevic (12/3/0) prompted a Chris Jans timeout and put Xavier in a spot where they were well and truly in the driver's seat. The test from there was one of game management. Mississippi State cranked up the pressure and tried to make Xavier guard someone other than Hubbard, who was hounded off the litany of ball screens the Bulldogs ran for him all night. The only time it really threatened to get interesting was when Mississippi State cut the lead back to 12 with 14:26 to play, but Xavier responded with a quick 6-0 run to put the Bulldogs back on the mat and it was never closer than 14 after that point. Xavier never took their foot off the gas, forced 13 second half turnovers, and gave the impression of a team that is comfortable playing with a lead against high major talent.

Xavier's defense has made a huge leap- In the past two seasons, Josh Hubbard has scored 12 or fewer points in 4 outings against high major competition. There was a moment in the first half when he started to heat up, but Xavier's size and aggression kept him off balance the rest of the night and forced one of the best scorers in the country into a line of 12/4/3 with 4 turnovers and 4-12/2-8/2-2 shooting. It is quite the reversal from getting carved up by guards blow Hubbard's level a year ago, including TJ Simpkins who had as many three point jump shooters fouled tonight as he did made baskets. Xavier wanted to get bigger in the portal, and that showed in the way they stifled the Bulldogs offense tonight, holding them to 0.8 points per possession.

The depth passed the first test- Xavier had the luxury of being able to play basically whoever they wanted in the first three games and knowing that it was probably going to work out for them. Tonight, the bench got shorter, but they still combined to chip in 34 points and give Xavier some big minutes. Chitikoudis ended up playing more minutes than Nwoko, taking 25 of the 40 at the center spot and was excellent if you ignore the column that tells you how well each player shot free throws. Kalek House couldn't get his shots falling, not for lack of trying, but ended the night with 4 boards, 3 assists, a block, a steal, and no turnovers in 21 minutes. Gabriel Pozzato only got 12 minutes, but managed to make a couple of huge shots in the run that gave Xavier the double digit lead they never lost. Rolyns Aligbe had a night to forget shooting wise, but 6 rebounds, a block, and a steal in 12 minutes is nothing to shake a stick at and Ruben Dominguez lost his starting spot, but responded with 9 points in 9 minutes on 2-3/2-3/3-3 shooting. It didn't all click for all these guys tonight, but the bench was a large reason why this one was such a comfortable win for X.

Tru Washington answered the bell- The biggest matchup was always going to be at the point guard position and Washington definitively won it. Tasked with his toughest task to date in a Xavier uniform, Washington responded by shutting down Hubbard and leading the game in points, rebounds, assists, and steals. It wasn't a one man show for X tonight, but there was a clear best player on the floor and it was Xavier's point guard. He was as demonstrative as he was excellent, clearly having taking it upon himself to lead the charge for Xavier in this game. There are a lot of new pieces on this roster, but the guy who has played more games for Richard Pitino than anyone else on Xavier set the tone for them all to follow tonight.

#2665. Miami Heat to host 2028 NBA All-Star Weekend, first time since 1990, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Miami is one of the sports world's most beloved event hosts. Super Bowls and National Championship Games are frequently held in South Florida, but for quite some time, the NBA's marquee regular-season event has been held elsewhere. The Miami Heat hosted All-Star Weekend in 1990, their second season in existence, but haven't hosted it since.

Well, that's about to change. Miami will host the event in 2028, after Phoenix does so in 2027, according to ESPN. The decision comes on the heels of widespread complaints about All-Star Weekends being held in smaller, less desirable cities to visit.

In 2024, The Oklahoman, questioning why Oklahoma City was not hosting the event, reported that the NBA planned to start enforcing minimums on certain amenities for prospective All-Star markets, including at least 7,250 hotel rooms and three five-star hotels, at least 650,000 square feet of convention center and exhibition space, and at least 75 nonstop domestic flights and at least 20 international flights. The NBA denied that these were ironclad requirements. Miami is the second city to earn an All-Star Weekend since that report, joining Phoenix, as San Francisco (2025) and Los Angeles (2026) were already settled. All four cities are notably relatively warm in February.

So, why did it take so long for Miami in particular to get a second All-Star Weekend? The answer may be the Miami International Boat Show, which occupies much of the city's hotel and convention space capacity and usually comes during Presidents' Day weekend, which often conflicts with the NBA's All-Star schedule. However, the Boat Show will reportedly be moving to a different weekend in 2028 to accommodate the NBA, which will hold All-Star Weekend from Feb. 18-20.

The Heat did not put in a bid to host All-Star Weekend, according to the Miami Herald, and have typically avoided doing so in the past. Instead, the NBA reportedly approached the Heat about hosting, and now, Miami will get its first All-Star Game in almost four decades.

#2662. Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo dominate Cavaliers in 133-121 loss in Miami

The Miami Heat probably salivated when they saw the injury report and noted the lack of bigs on the Cleveland Cavaliers' roster. Evan Mobley was announced out on Thursday with a toe injury. Early on, it looked as if they would be able to survive his absence on Friday night. However, as the game progressed in Miami, the issues only compounded.

Despite a decent scoring night from James Harden (20 points) and Donovan Mitchell (25 points), the Cavaliers' offense was too dependent on outside shooting. The Cavaliers were relying heavily on one big man on the floor throughout the game. Against most teams, this might be a fine approach. However, the Heat boast a lineup with Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo.

The Heat's All-Star duo gave the Cavaliers fits all night, running downhill and providing a huge problem that they just didn't have the personnel to stop. The Cavs were constantly having their smaller wings and guards tossed into switches that would see them in mismatches that resulted in good looks for both Giannis and Bam.

The Cavaliers, without Mobley's defensive presence, were not up to the task. Bam (37 points on 13-for-19 shooting) and Giannis (37 points on 15-for-20 shooting) heavily contributed to the Heat's 54 points in the paint. The Cavaliers were not able to generate nearly enough offense inside to match Miami's output, scoring 40 points in the paint by comparison.

There were some bright spots for the Cavaliers. Tyrese Proctor (22 points), Meleek Thomas (12 points), and Jaylon Tyson (16 points) all contributed with timely buckets and reliable shooting on a night where the Cavaliers were playing catch-up for the whole second half.

A loss like this stings. It felt like they were generating positive momentum and turning the page from the early season struggles after their big win against the New York Knicks. However, losing Mobley and facing an imposing frontcourt like Miami's halted any forward progress.

The Cavaliers look to turn the page when they face the Dallas Mavericks Saturday night in Cleveland.

#2657. Diving deeper into Cavs 133-121 loss to Heat: Supporting players shine in losing effort

Facing a front line of Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo is a tall task for any team — especially one without the services of Evan Mobley (toe). The Miami Heat's ability to attack the depleted frontcourt led to a 133-121 loss for the Cleveland Cavaliers.

37 points on 15-of-20 shooting, 9 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 block

Typically, the Cavs use Jarrett Allen as the primary defender on Giannis, with Mobley shading in his direction to provide help at the rim. Without Mobley, Allen was left on an island guarding Giannis without much help behind him. Allen fought hard, but he could only do so much.

The Heat have struggled as a team this season, but those issues haven't come at the expense of Giannis's individual numbers. He's still been playing at a superstar level.

37 points on 13-0f-19 shooting, 14 rebounds, 3 assists

Peyton Watson drew the primary assignment on Adebayo with Mobley sidelined. Watson needed to help on Giannis drives and was giving up considerable strength in his individual matchup with Adebayo. These two factors allowed Adebayo to get whatever he wanted inside, as evidenced by shooting 9-of- 12 in the paint.

25 points on 9-of-21 shooting, 7 assists, 4 rebounds

This was a good game from a process perspective. Mitchell got rid of the ball when traps came his way, and trusted his teammates when he needed to. Miami's defense was collapsing inside on any dribble penetration, leaving room for outside shots. Mitchell took advantage of this, going 8-for-17 on jump shots. The issue came on drives and floaters inside, where he was just 1-for-4.

Anything bought from the links helps support Fear the Sword. You can buy the comfortable Cavs hoodie HERE. You can also shop all of Homage's Cavs gear HERE.

4 points on 2-of-10 shooting, 4 rebounds, 2 assists

This was a tough matchup for Watson. He was asked to guard a player he had no business defending due to injuries and, unsurprisingly, struggled. The issue was that he couldn't take advantage of Miami's propensity to shrink the floor on the other end.

Watson's frustrations from the outside continued in Miami. He went 0-for-5 from three on a night when the Cavs desperately needed some additional floor spacing.

The process hasn't been an issue for Watson. He's taking the right shots and doing some encouraging things on the defensive end, but the results just haven't consistently been there.

22 points on 7-of-9 shooting, 4 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 steal

Proctor has been coming into his own over the past week. At the start of the season, he seemed hesitant to put the ball on the floor and attack as a scorer when given opportunities. That has gradually shifted in recent games, culminating in an impressive offensive performance in Miami.

On Friday, Proctor was hunting for his outside shot. He didn't hesitate when the ball swung to him on the perimeter. That's the confidence the Cavs need from someone who should get plenty of open looks given the attention the starting guards draw.

The version of Proctor we've seen over the past few games is indeed a rotation player. At this point, the question is whether he can still maintain that confidence in all aspects of his offensive game when he isn't shooting as well as he has recently.

"Bam and Giannis kind of had their way with us."

– Kenny Atkinson on what went wrong in this game

You're just not winning a game like this when Miami's front court combines for 74 points.

The Miami Heat were in the 98th percentile for offensive rating this tgame (137.1).

Miami dominated inside. They retrieved 34.8% of their missed shots (73rd percentile), had a free-throw rate of 33 (85th percentile), and scored 56 points in the paint. Controlling the paint and forcing your way to the free-throw line is still the most effective way to generate a great offense.

As easy as it would be to blame the Cavs for these issues, sometimes you just have to tip your cap to the other team. Miami had the personnel to take advantage of Cleveland's injuries, and they did.

Zach Lowe made a good point on his most recent pod that I believe is worth expounding on: The Cavs have slowly been evolving their identity.

Cleveland found out in their 2025 series with the Indiana Pacers that they need more well-rounded players who can pass, dribble, and shoot.

Their initial effort in identifying those supporting pieces didn't necessarily work out (Lonzo Ball), but their recent attempts have been much more encouraging. Guys like Peyton Watson, Mario Hezonja, Meleek Thomas, and Tyrese Proctor can fill multiple roles on the court and are more than just specialists. Jaylon Tyson also fits that box, although he was drafted before the Pacers series. This archetype stands in stark contrast with previous supporting players like Dean Wade, Georges Niang, De'Andre Hunter, and Keon Ellis, who were more specialized in one particular skill.

Quietly, the Cavs have shifted from a team with specialists around their core players to one where their core is insulated with more well-rounded skill sets.

It made sense to put specialists around the Cavs in 2023. That team desperately needed more shooting around the original core four after Mitchell's first season in Cleveland. It's nearly impossible to win playoff series if you can't spread the floor in any meaningful way. Prioritizing shooting allowed them to advance in the playoffs in subsequent years, but if they intend to take the next step, they needed to diversify their rotation players.

Early injuries to Sam Merrill and Nae'Qwan Tomlin have given some of the newer supporting players more room to shine, and they've taken advantage of it. Against the New York Knicks, it was Thomas and Proctor who carried them through some of those bench lineups, and it was Watson who made the game-saving block. Here, it was Proctor who provided consistent scoring, Thomas (12 points) who supplied some shot-making at the end of the third to get them back into the game, and Tyson (16 points) who filled in well as a starter.

The Cavs are still figuring some things out, and are far from a finished product. But if you wanted something positive to hang your hat on early in the season, it's the fact that the supporting pieces have the potential to change how this team plays.

Stars still matter. The Cavs will have a tough time winning playoff series this spring if Mitchell or Harden lay an egg. But the emergence of some of these supporting pieces has the potential to change what is asked of the stars during close postseason games. Maybe Thomas can carry some of the scoring load for stretches in the second and third quarters. Maybe Watson's ability to recover defensively alters how the two-big front line operates defensively and further insulates the guards. Maybe Proctor can help bring the ball up against the press, alleviating that burden from the stars.

The Cavs didn't get the win on Friday. Trying to defend a Giannis-led team without Mobley is a tall task. Results notwithstanding, we've seen some encouraging steps forward from some of the supporting cast the last week or so. That could make a huge difference if the stars can get healthy and more in sync than they have been.

#2656. At least 50 different quarterbacks will have started games through Week 10

Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza will make his first career start on Sunday. Two others will make their debuts, too: Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck and Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord.

Via NBC Sports research, they'll become the 48th, 49th, and 50th different quarterbacks to start games during the 2026 season.

It will be only the second time in the last 15 years (excluding the 1987 strike season) during which 50 different quarterbacks have started games in the first 10 weeks of a season.

If, for some reason, another quarterback makes his first start of the season on Sunday (that's unlikely with Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock not having an injury designation for Sunday), it will be the second-most starters through 10 weeks since 1950.

In 1999, 55 different quarterbacks started games through the first 10 weeks of the season.

Most of the changes have arisen from injury. For the Raiders, the transition to Mendoza happened after Kirk Cousins was traded to the Vikings.

#2655. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2654. Castle scores season-high 32 points as Spurs stop the Warriors 123-85 for 11th straight win

SAN ANTONIO (AP) — Stephon Castle scored a season-high 32 points, Victor Wembanyama had 12 points and 12 rebounds and the San Antonio Spurs won their 11th straight game, rolling past the Golden State Warriors 123-85 Friday night to remain unbeaten in NBA Cup play.

Golden State's only double-figure scorers were L.J. Cryer with 20 points and Charles Bassey with 11.

The Warriors are without Stephen Curry, who is sidelined at least two weeks with a right oblique tear suffered in a 115-108 loss in Houston on Wednesday. Golden State could have used a banner scoring night from the two-time MVP to overcome this lopsided loss.

The Spurs led by 43 points in the third quarter, allowing the defending Western Conference champions to sit their starters and most of their key reserves for the entire fourth.

Wembanyama was 5 for 11 from the field and 0 for 2 on 3-pointers while playing only 21 minutes and collecting his 121st career double-double.

Warriors forward Draymond Green was issued a Flagrant Foul 1 for a forearm shove from behind off a running start that sent Wembanyama tumbling out of bounds with 6:47 remaining in the first half.

Green, who exited and did not return in the first half after the Flagrant 1, finished with four points, three rebounds and three assists in 16 minutes.

Golden State was 5 for 25 from the field in the opening quarter as San Antonio raced to a 38-14 lead. It was the fewest points scored in any quarter by a Spurs opponent this season, as well as a season low for the Warriors.

Golden State trailed 63-33 at the half, the fewest points by a San Antonio opponent in the first half since Phoenix had 31 on Feb. 7, 2018.

Castle shot 12 for 18 and was 5 for 8 on 3-pointers. He surpassed his previous high of 24 points against Oklahoma City on opening night on a slam dunk off an alley-oop pass on a finger roll from Wembanyama.

#2653. Champions Classic NBA Draft guide: Who scouts will be watching in college basketball's high-profile showcase

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The most anticipated double-header of the young college basketball season takes place tonight in Chicago as No. 2 Duke meets No. 5 Michigan State, followed by No. 15 Kansas vs. No. 24 Kentucky in the Champions Classic.

The event is also expected to draw a heavy dose of NBA scouts and decision-makers to Chicago, given the opportunity to see so many high-level prospects under one roof on one night.

One wrinkle: The best NBA prospect on the court Tuesday night won't even be eligible to be drafted in 2027. That's Duke freshman Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje who is 17 years old and won't turn 18 until next May. In order to be eligible for the NBA Draft, a player must be at least 19 years old during the calendar year of the draft, per NBA rules.

So not only will Boumtje Boumtje be ineligible for the upcoming draft; he is expected back at Duke for his sophomore season.

Another thing to keep in mind is that these NBA scouts and executives will use what they see on Tuesday night as a benchmark and something to measure against for the rest of the season. They will not over-index on what they see on just one given night.

The public, on the other hand, has a tendency to fall for that trap. Because tonight is so visible, if someone has a glaring performance (good or bad), it often anchors a lot of the public discourse for the rest of the season. Trevor Keels is the classic example. He scored 25 points in the 2021 Champions Classic, was mocked as a lottery pick almost immediately afterwards, ended up declaring for the draft prematurely, and slipped to the second round.

The moral of the story – keep what you see on Tuesday night in perspective, because the people who make the big decisions certainly will.

So with all that in mind, here's a look at the top NBA prospects from the four teams in action at the Champions Classic

This shouldn't come as a surprise, but the Blue Devils lead the way in terms of total NBA prospects. What's interesting about this year's team though, is that their best prospect, Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje, isn't even eligible this year, but is the early favorite to be the top pick in 2028. Boumtje Boumtje has a combination of size and skill, which is unmatched for his age, not just in college basketball, but anywhere in the world.

Ngongba had a chance to be a first-round pick a year ago, but opted to return to Duke, and so far, it looks a decision that is going to pay off. Ngonba fits a coveted NBA archetype in that he's a mismatch five-man who can play inside and out. He is a vertical spacer, reliable passer, and consistent offensive rebounder who has massive length to also be a rim protector. Scouts want to see him take the next step as a shot-blocker and as a rebounder while proving his durability.

If Ngongba can prove he can space the floor with his shooting, that's just an added bonus. He's prepared for that challenge by getting himself into the best shape of his career and looks poised to be the focal point for the Blue Devils, at least on the interior, this season. In short, it's early, but the lottery is very much in play here.

Sarr is a long and athletic big wing who, last year as a freshman, was already one of the best perimeter defenders in the ACC, if not the country. This year, he's going to get the volume to show his offensive growth. So far, that's come more in transition and as a secondary playmaker, but what the NBA is going to be most interested in is his ability to make spot-up 3s in order to fit that coveted 3-and-D archetype. Sarr was 32% from that range last season, but hasn't even attempted a three through two games this year, but has gotten to the free-throw line in high volume and made 71%, after connecting on only 53% last year.

While the progression of Sarr's total game is important, scouts will be monitoring the shooting most closely all year long. Duke also appears to be recruiting as if they expect Sarr to move on after the year. The first-round should be the expectation, with the late lottery not being out of the question.

Williams has quickly become one of the most polarizing draft prospects in the country. He was a top five recruit out of the high school ranks a year ago because of his combination of size, athleticism, fluidity, skill, and shot-blocking potential, even with real questions about his physicality.

Williams has played a limited role to start the season and could fall further out of the rotation as games get closer. Nevertheless, it wouldn't be at all surprising to see him explore professional opportunities, even if this season doesn't go as expected. It also wouldn't be unprecedented to see a team invest a first-round pick in trying to develop his tools, even in that scenario. It's a trajectory that could mirror that of Peyton Watson, who was a prized 2021 recruit who didn't play much in his freshman season at UCLA, still declared for the draft, and ended up being the 30th pick for the Nuggets a year later. That pick has gone down as a very good one.

If the exhibition slate was any indication, Blackwell may be Duke's most reliable player this season. He came to Durham after putting up 19 points and 5 rebounds on 43/39/86 shooting last year for Wisconsin, but did not get any first-round traction in the pre-draft process.

The narrative once Blackwell hit the portal was that he wanted to play with the ball in his hands. Fortunately, he seems to have gotten over that, because his path to the NBA is based on proving he can be a reliable two-way role player, not an alpha creator. Duke is the biggest stage to prove that. If the shooting splits hold up and he can provide some secondary playmaking and be a defensive asset, then hopefully scouts won't be so worried about his lack of length come the next draft cycle.

NBA scouts are also watching: Deron Rippey Jr., 6-1, freshman, guard; Bryson Howard, 6-4, freshman, guard; Caleb Foster, 6-4, senior, guard; Cayden Boozer, 6-3, sophomore, guard.

The Spartans are unlike many of college basketball's other top programs in that while they are projected to be among the very best teams in the sport, but they don't have as many glaring NBA prospects. Of course, similar claims used to be made about Villanova teams of old, and that proved to be beyond shortsighted, so it's possible that time will prove the masses wrong about the individual talent on this year's team.

Fears is undoubtedly one of the best players and floor generals in all of college basketball. Everything Michigan State does begins with him, and the same was true last year for a team that won 27 games and advanced to the Sweet 16 before running into UConn. There are, however, questions about how his game translates to the NBA. He lacks ideal measurables for the league, doesn't have the outlier burst to compensate, and is also a questionable shooter.

Still, it's hard to bet against Fears' will, and so chances are he figures out how to stick at the next level. The elephant in the room, though, is that while he is a true senior this year at Michigan State, his earning potential will almost certainly be higher in college than the pros next year. The Spartans have recruited as if he's not going to be back, but if and when financial reality hits, will they be willing to tolerate seeing him in another uniform? Only time will tell.

The baby-faced sophomore is still a work in progress and just starting to grow into his body and fill out his frame. Right now, he is much more of a Robin to Fears' Batman for the Spartans. And yet, Scott has a game that could ultimately translate to the next level more seamlessly. He's a big wing with positional size, a reliable floor-spacer who made 37% of his threes last year as a freshman. He's also a reliable decision-maker who turned the ball over a total of 32 times in 729 minutes a year ago. In short, the NBA is intrigued, so whether or not it's this year or down the road, Scott is on the right trajectory.

NBA scouts are also watching: Coen Carr, 6-6, senior, forward; Jasiah Jervis, 6-4, freshman, guard; Ethan Taylor, 7-2, freshman, center.

For the second consecutive year, Bill Self has a freshman with a chance to prove he should be the top pick in the draft. The biggest question for most of the summer, though, was based on who else they could get to surround Tyran Stokes. Now, thanks to eligibility being granted to Melvin Council, Tre White, and Tre Kaufman-Renn, the Jayhawks suddenly have an ideal supporting cast. Here's the thing, though: if those guys were NBA players at this point, they wouldn't have been available to return.

Stokes is the early favorite to be the top pick in the 2027 NBA draft. He's built like a throwback power forward, but can initiate like a guard, not just for himself, but for others as well. The biggest questions in high school were about his approach and ability to impact winning on a daily basis, but so far at Kansas, he's gotten rave reviews. Being surrounded by veterans no doubt helps, as does having some reinforcements. When Stokes dropped 27 points, eight rebounds, and seven assists on Duke in an exhibition, it was a sign of things to come. That performance came without the Jayhawks having yet established an ideal scheme to get him going in space and movement. In short, if Stokes' mindset stays the same, he has a chance to distance himself from the field this season, and that process could begin tonight.

NBA scouts are also watching: Taylen Kinney, 6-2, freshman, guard; Keanu Dawes, 6-9, senior, forward; Melvin Council Jr, 6-4, graduate, guard; Tre White, 6-6, graduate, wing; Trey Kaufman-Renn, 6-8, graduate, center/forward.

Malachi Moreno and Milan Momcilovic both had a good chance to be drafted last June. So, when they opted to return, it wasn't for a lack of options; it was for the valuation that college basketball, and Kentucky in particular, was able to pay them. That's a very different calculus than graduate students who return after not signing NBA contracts. So, while this year's roster may not have any glaring lottery picks, it does have pro talent.

Moreno fits a coveted archetype in today's NBA because he has legit size and can be reliable in offensive structure. He's a quick processor of the game and a reliable decision-maker at various spots on the floor. He's a solid passer, efficient finisher, and may even have some long-term shooting potential. He also provides some defensive rim protection, but could certainly help his stock this season by becoming more assertive around the rim on both ends of the floor. The first-round should be the goal for Moreno coming out of this season.

Momcilovic was one of the best shooters in college basketball last year, making 49% of his threes on almost 8 attempts per game, while also making 88% of his free throws for good measure. Through two games at Kentucky, he's getting even more volume, with 17 attempted threes in just two games so far. While his floor-spacing gravity is not in doubt, the questions for the next level are more about his ability to defend his position without putting his team in rotation. So, all-year scouts will be locked in on some of the nuances of Momcilovic's game, like his foot speed, angles, and rotations. Long-term, Momcilovic has positional size and a translatable niche, but may be in a familiar spot in the off-season, with more guaranteed money in the college ranks.

Wilkins was one of the best mid-major freshmen in the country last year, posting nearly 18 points and 5 assists for a Furman that went to the NCAA Tournament. He's a classic late-bloomer who had an undeveloped, wiry frame in high school, but quickly started to put things together as he grew into his body.

While he's still filling out, Wilkins is naturally smooth with real playmaking genes. Through two games at Kentucky, there's also been an early uptick in his shooting (he's 5-for-11 from three and 6-for-6 from the free-throw line). If that growth is sustainable, he'll continue to build momentum with NBA decision-makers. Exactly what his timeline will be, though, still remains to be seen.

NBA scouts are also watching: Kam Williams, 6-7, junior, wing; Zoom Diallo, 6-5, junior, guard; Mason Williams, 6-2, freshman, guard

#2651. Game Day: Louisville at North Carolina

Location: Kenan Stadium: Chapel Hill, N.C.

Announcers: Mike Couzens (play-by-play), Tom Luginbill (analyst), and Lauren Sisler (sidelines)

Last Meeting: Louisville won 47-35 on Sept. 9, 2017 in Chapel Hill

Bill Belichick had a poor start to his tenure at UNC last year, with the main issues being on the offensive side of the ball. He remedied that issue this year by going out and hiring none other than Bobby Petrino to be his offensive coordinator. Petrino had been bouncing around at a few spots since being fired by Louisville, but his offensive acumen is still coveted. The Tar Heels have improved on offense, though they still rank toward the bottom of the rankings in some key offensive metrics.

As always, an offense is only as good as its quarterback, and the Tar Heels are average with Billy Edwards under center. The veteran transfer quarterback has played about as well as most expected him to this season. His inconsistent play has been an issue for this offense, and it has contributed to a couple of the losses this year.

As the season has gone on, he has played better, with his last two games being his best. He torched Miami's defense for four touchdowns while completing 82% of his passes. He came back the following weekend to complete 76% of his passes against a solid UConn team. Edwards isn't one of the top quarterbacks Louisville has seen this season, but he has played like one recently.

UNC has three running backs that they can rely on, and they play all three of them. Demon June leads the group in touchdowns with 8 on the season. Benjamin Hall leads the group in yards and yards per carry. Jaylin Mcgill leads the group in yards per play as he is a factor as a receiver out of the backfield. They are all over 220 pounds, and Petrino has done a good job of utilizing them this season. The staff likes to ride the hot hand with this group, so we will have to wait to see which player gets the most touches.

Louisville will face another opponent that has a single key player at the wide receiver position this weekend. Jordan Shipp is one of the more talented players the Cards will face this year, and they will need to have a plan. Shipp has good size at 6-2/200, and he can really move. He is a fluid athlete with good body control which he uses to make contested catches and catches in tight spots. He is not a burner in the open field, but he has plenty of speed to score on a long play if he gets open.

The biggest threat on this offense is at tight end in Jelani Thurman. Lincoln Keinholz' former teammate at Ohio State has had a similar situation as he did not make much of an impact for the Buckeyes, but he has emerged as one of the best tight ends in the country for UNC. He has already set the school record for touchdowns by a tight end with 8, which is the most in the country among tight ends. He also ranks in the top five in just about every receiving category when it comes to tight ends.

This team doesn't create a lot of big passing plays, but when they do it is down the middle of the field to Thurman, or because he pulls defenders with him. Petrino is known for working deep over routes throughout his career, but this team has killed teams down the seams. Louisville's defense has been victimized many times on seam routes this year, so they will need to adjust their plan from their normal reliance on Cover 3.

The UNC offensive line has been pretty average this year, especially from a run blocking standpoint. They don't allow a lot of penetration, but they haven't been opening massive holes for the running backs, either. Where they have struggled is being consistent in pass protection. Billy Edwards is just a big better than being a statue in the pocket, so he is not one to avoid the rush if it gets to him. It has not helped that his line has struggled with speed rushers this year. The Cards should have an opportunity to get pressure this weekend.

Defense is Bill Belichick's forte, and the North Carolina Tar Heels are benefiting from his expertise this year. For the second straight year, Belichick has his defense ranked in the top 50 in yards per play. His group is being led by his son Brian after his son Steve left the team earlier this season. While the defense has taken a step back this year, they have played well enough to keep the Tar Heels in each game, and they've made big plays at big moments.

The most talented group on this team is the defensive line, with a couple of NFL prospects. Melkart Abou Jaoude is the returning ACC leader in sacks, while Jaylen Harvey has been a very good addition from Penn State with 21 pressures this season. The edges of this defense haven't put up crazy numbers from a havoc standpoint, but they will be key players for this defense if Louisville continues to attack the edges of the defense.

The interior of the line is where this defense is at its best. Xavier Lewis is one of the best defensive tackles in the country. He is in the top five in pressures, tackles for loss, and sacks among his position group. The 6-0/260 tackle is extremely undersized, but he is very quick, and he uses his quickness to beat blocks to get into the backfield. He will be a key player in this game and will likely cause some issues for Louisville's offensive line.

Isaiah Johnson and Leroy Jackson are the other top players on the interior of the defense. Jackson has 14 pressures on the season as the main backup for Lewis, but he and Johnson provide really good size on the inside as well. Johnson is big enough to demand a double team, which has been a factor in Lewis' big season. He has been able to get one-on-one matchups often, and that has not gone well for offensive linemen.

UNC's linebackers have benefited more than just about anyone from the strong play of the defensive line. Derek McDonald and Peyton Sheelmann are averaging 19 tackles a game between the two of them. Both players are ranked in the top 25 in tackles nationally, and they are constantly running free when you watch their games. Louisville has adapted their running game over the last few weeks, but they will likely have a hard time running the stretch zone runs that they really like. These two guys can run, and they will have a lot of space to get downhill to make tackles behind the line.

Jaiden Patterson leads a solid cornerback group that has played at an average level this season. UNC has given up a lot of yardage this season, but they are better when it comes to metrics like passer rating. The corners have had some issues against the top players they've seen this year. Umari Hatcher, Jordon Faison, Calvin Russell, and Bryant Wesco all stood out to me when I watched their games. Those receivers were able to get open and make big plays on the outside.

The biggest playmaker outside of the defensive linemen is Greg Smith at free safety. He leads the team with 3 interceptions this year, and he's at his best as a deep safety playing center field. Smith can also come down into the box in run support or cover if needed. He's having one of the best seasons in the ACC at safety. While this secondary isn't great, they do have a couple of players who can make a play on the ball, which is not something I would say about the last few opponents for the Cards.

Not easy to find non-basketball tweets from the UNC crowd.

Give me an SMU win over Wake at noon and a Cards win in Chapel Hill, and the EL is probably back up to where we want it to be for next week's home/conference finale against Pitt.

#2650. Re-grading the Jaylen Brown-Paul George trade: Celtics' grade has greatly improved, 76ers' mark stays perfect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Besides the Luka Dončić stunner, you could argue that this summer's Jaylen Brown blockbuster was the most surprising trade in recent NBA history. A former Finals MVP coming off of his best season traded for ... Paul George? Someone widely treated as one of the NBA's worst contracts and half of the draft capital a superstar typically fetches? The reactions were, obviously, extreme. Celtics fans revolted. Pundits expected a meaningful drop-off for Boston. Trade graders like myself pilloried Brad Stevens and his front office for moving a 29-year-old All-NBA forward for what appeared to be far less than fair value.

And yet, as Brown prepares to face his former employer for the first time, the two teams sit neck-and-neck in the Eastern Conference. The 76ers top the standings at 9-2. The Celtics are right behind them at 8-2, but have the East's best net rating at +11.6. While Philadelphia has thus far gotten exactly what it wanted out of the trade, the Celtics seemingly have as well. So with their first of potentially many high-stakes clashes this season set for Tuesday night (8 p.m. ET, NBC/fubo), let's revisit the trade and hand out revised grades for the offseason's most impactful trade.

The backlash to the George-for-Brown trade was fundamentally centered on two premises:

The first premise was, frankly, outdated in the apron era. Yes, Kevin Durant netted four first-round picks, a first-round swap, and players who would go on to net six additional first-round picks and another swap, but that was all the way back in February 2023, and that trade completely derailed Phoenix's future. The James Harden trade played out similarly for the Nets. Teams are more skittish about all-in moves for older players than they've ever been.

There have been outlier, extremely high-cost trades since then, but all came under somewhat irreplicable circumstances. Mikal Bridges netted five first-round picks and a swap, for instance, but he never misses games, came with two years of cheap cost-control and played collegiately with several other key Knicks. New York viewed him as the finishing piece of a championship team, and the Knicks were ultimately proven correct.

Desmond Bane wasn't as underpaid, but he fit the extremely narrow niche the Magic needed: someone who could enhance their offense without commanding high usage on a team that was already locked into two max-salary shot-creators or compromising their defensive identity. There were maybe a handful of players in the NBA Orlando could have targeted for that role, and Bane, amazingly, was probably the only one available. In an extremely injured Eastern Conference, the Magic tried to be opportunistic. That's where these lopsided trades happen. They're almost always circumstantial.

The more typical star trade scenario is something closer to what the Milwaukee Bucks went through with Giannis Antetokounmpo. The player is older, attempts to fix things internally have failed, and the relationship between star and team is no longer tenable. The acquiring team typically has a leverage advantage, and that's especially true in the apron era, where paying the sort of giant salaries these stars get in their early 30s carries far more risk than reward. Antetokounmpo netted three picks, one swap and a handful of players that won't be foundational for the Bucks. We know Antetokounmpo had more trade value than Brown because the Celtics tried to trade Brown and more for Antetokounmpo, but a deal wasn't struck. So if Antetokounmpo, a two-time MVP, was worth three-and-a-half picks plus some player value, Brown being worth two picks and some player value feels in line with the new, cost-conscious NBA.

And then of course, there's the matter of what the player value actually was. That brings us to George. From November through January of last season, George averaged just 16 points on 42-38-86 shooting. This was in line with his 2024-25 performance, and together, the year-and-a-half sample felt reliable for an aging star. Well, George then got suspended 25 games. When he returned in March, he was a 21-point scorer on better shooting splits who looked rejuvenated defensively. He went on to torch the Celtics in the first round of the playoffs. Most of us expected George to look more like the player he was before that suspension in Boston. The Celtics bet that he would look like who he was after, and thus far, they've looked correct.

The raw numbers are superb: 20.4 points, 47-43-81 shooting and his highest assist and rebounding rates since he left the Clippers. The fit has been even better. Much was made of how low many advanced metrics are on Brown relative to his reputation, but the more significant story here was always his outlier status within Boston's intended team structure. Joe Mazzulla wants to maximize 3-point attempt rate. George's 3-point attempt rate so far this season (51.4%) is nearly twice Brown's (27.8%). Brad Stevens spoke openly about not wanting to concentrate usage in two players, and George's usage rate is nearly eight percentage points lower than Brown's was a year ago. The Celtics wanted this sort of player in their system and next to Jayson Tatum, and it's working.

Yet just as vitally, George is helping the Celtics diversify a bit as a team. The Celtics generated the second-fewest turnovers in the NBA last season. They're averaging the eighth-most in the NBA thus far this season, and George is the single biggest reason why. Only Dyson Daniels and Scottie Barnes are averaging more deflections, and among players who have played at least four games, only Daniels and Kris Dunn are generating more steals.

The Celtics had the lowest free-throw attempt rate in the NBA last season as well. They're right around the middle of the pack this year. Tatum is the one drawing most of those fouls, but George is a critical part of the structure that gets Tatum to the line. Brown can be a bit of a ball-stopper. Among true forwards, only Kawhi Leonard and Zion Williamson averaged more seconds per touch than Brown a year ago. The average George touch this season lasts 3.3 seconds compared to just under five for Brown a year ago. It's simply easier to compromise a defense when the ball is moving and players are making quick decisions. That's how defenses are forced into rotation and wind up fouling out of desperation. As a team, the Celtics have the sixth-lowest average time per touch this season compared to the eighth-highest a year ago.

Even the contract feels a bit more palatable now than it did at the time. Brown would have become eligible for an extension on his supermax contract last offseason, and based on the season he had, he would have been more than justified in asking for one. The Celtics, clearly, had no plans to commit extra years to Brown on top of the three that he was already owed. George isn't quite living up to his supermax price tag thus far this season, but his deal is a year shorter and comes with no such extension pressure.

If anything, his player option for next season opens some interesting doors for the Celtics if they decide they're happy with this partnership. As of right now, the Celtics have around $3 million in first-apron room for the 2027-28 season based on current projections. Say they want to use the full mid-level exception on a free agent or perhaps need a bit more wiggle room to make a trade. They could theoretically go to George and ask him to lower his cap figure in exchange for another year of security. Turning a one-year, $56.6 million deal into, say, a two-year, $90 million deal could make sense for both sides provided George sustains this level of play.

The reasonable fear that he might not is why we stop at a "B-" for Boston. This is still his age-36 season. George has been injury-prone for most of his career. He presumably will not get a 25-game break this season, and even if he's this good all year, all of these benefits he's brought to Boston are somewhat regular-season-centric. The playoffs are a different game, one that leans much more into Brown's strengths as an individual shotmaker and man-to-man defender. The Celtics still never get to the rim. Their best answer for opposing star guards is probably Jordan Walsh, whose offense makes him hard to play for too long. If Boston flames out in the playoffs, we might view Brown's absence as one of the bigger reasons why. The path to actually winning this trade gets paved in April and May.

But for now, at least, it's starting to make sense. The Celtics added two premium draft assets in a way that allowed them to maintain their existing playing style and avoid taking a major step back in the present. They sidestepped what probably would have been an ugly contract negotiation, and the more barbs get traded in the press, the clearer it becomes that this situation simply was not salvageable. The Celtics had to trade Brown. The offers were far lower than we anticipated. Boston still managed to make the best of less-than-ideal circumstances and still factors prominently into the Eastern Conference championship picture.

Funnily enough, you could pretty easily argue that George would actually be a far better fit for this iteration of the 76ers than Brown is. Philadelphia's 20th-ranked offense has a bottom-five 3-point attempt rate and the eighth-highest average seconds per touch in the NBA. The Sixers could stand to trade some of that dribbling for a bit more shooting. Considering how lethal their transition offense can be, George's turnover generation would also fit this defense like a glove. The 76ers will get better offensively. We're still in tiny-sample season, and everyone's still learning how to play together. But George is undeniably the easier player to fit onto a roster like this than Brown.

Of course, the 76ers wouldn't have a roster like this without Brown. Widespread reporting has made it clear that Philadelphia's acquisition of Brown was what first caught the attention of LeBron James in free agency. If Brown was indeed a swing factor in the 76ers getting LeBron, that assuages any short-term salary concerns for Brown. For God's sake, the Philadelphia 76ers have LeBron James on a minimum contract. Even if Brown is overpaid, the surplus value on the James contract more than offsets any negative value there.

The 76ers have far less reason to fear an extension than Boston did as well. By trading Brown, the Celtics subjected him to the NBA's six-month extend-and-trade restrictions. That meant he could only tack one year onto his contract rather than two, and because he has multiple years remaining on his contract, he's not eligible to extend during the season. The 76ers therefore get to table those discussions until the offseason at the earliest, and remember, at that point, Brown will be negotiating off of the more modest statistics that come with sacrificing for the sake of a superteam. It's simply easier to envision Brown extending at less than the max in Philadelphia than it would have been in Boston.

Speaking of sacrificing, remember the whole "Jaylen Brown wants his own team" narrative from last offseason? For all we know, it was true at the time and might have remained true had he stayed with the Celtics. So far, that has been a complete non-issue for the 76ers. Brown is currently sporting his lowest usage rate since 2020 (before he became an All-Star). He's turning the ball over around half as often per 100 possessions as he did a season ago. He's an enormous part of a defense that surprisingly ranks No. 6 in the NBA so far this season. He's even openly called the 76ers Tyrese Maxey's team.

And the 76ers are, obviously, winning. They're mostly winning clutch games, but hey, you expect to win close games with four stars in your starting lineup. They're going to figure out the finer points of maximizing this talent mix over time, but even the "getting to know each other" version of this group poses almost impossible matchup problems for other teams. Take Cleveland, who has already faced Philadelphia twice. Can you guess which two Cavalier defenders have spent the most partial possessions guarding Brown, per NBA.com tracking data? James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, at 60.6 combined. Those are the sort of defenders you try to hide on weak scorers to preserve for offense. Well, where exactly are Harden and Mitchell supposed to hide against this team? There are no weak spots. The advantage of having this many creators is that Philadelphia basically starts every possession with an exploitable mismatch.

On pure talent accumulation alone, this is the sort of roster teams tend to go all-in for. Philadelphia didn't even have to. While the Stepien Rule complicates the tradability of some of their remaining picks, the 76ers are still slated to have four first-round picks in the next seven drafts. There is still ammunition for some sort of pivot here, whether that's a short-term upgrade to maximize this title run or more likely, some sort of long-term change at center as Joel Embiid gets older and potentially less reliable from a health perspective.

There are going to be depth questions down the line. Even if Brown gets less than a 35% max on his eventual extension, he's going to be pricey. Maxey feels like a near-lock for a supermax extension in the years to come, and while VJ Edgecombe will almost certainly be limited to 25% of the cap on his rookie extension, he'll still account for quite a bit of money. The 76ers are a top-heavy roster today, and that's after hitting a few home runs on the margins and getting arguably the greatest player of all time to take the minimum. Sustaining contention beyond the "Embiid is still a matchup nightmare and LeBron is on the team" era is going to require near-perfect management on the margins.

But this isn't rocket science. How many teams have a trio they can feel better about for, say, the next three-to-five years than Maxey, Brown and Edgecombe? The Brown trade opened an immediate championship window and likely ensured a relatively high baseline for the rest of the decade, assuming acceptable health and wise decisions elsewhere on the roster. It was a great trade in July and it remains a great trade today.

#2645. Group of retired MLB umpires, including Joe West, file lawsuit alleging they are owed more than $2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former MLB umpire Joe West is part of a group of five retired umpires who are suing their pension plan and alleging they have been underpaid by the plan, the Associated Press reports. West, along with Tom Hallion, Gerry Davis, Larry Vanover, and Jerry Layne, filed the suit in late September in federal court in New York.

The suit alleges that the five umpires have been underpaid by the pension plan by more than $2 million. According to the AP, the suit "was filed against the American Leagues and National Leagues of Professional Baseball Clubs Retirement Income Plan for Umpires and that entity's retirement committee." The five umpires claim their benefits were not calculated correctly and therefore should receive additional money.

West, 74, retired from umpiring in MLB in 2021 after umpiring more than 5,000 games at the highest level starting in 1976. The man they called "Cowboy Joe" umpired a record 5,460 games in all, was known as a colorful figure in the sport and sometimes even a source of controversy.

In 2021, West won more than $500,000 in damages as the result of a defamation suit against former MLB player Paul Lo Duca after Lo Duca alleged during a podcast that West would "open up the strike zone" for reliever Billy Wagner in exchange for driving one of Wagner's vintage cars.

West referenced his "history with lawsuits" on Thursday. From the AP:

West said that when he brought up the issue to the retirement committee, he was offered a relatively small sum. West said MLB senior vice president and chief employment counsel Steven Gonzalez told him: "If you don't like the number, sue us."

"Does Steve Gonzalez not know my history with dealing with lawsuits?" West said.

Like West, Davis also retired after the 2021 season while Hallion umpired through the 2022 season and Layne and Vanover stepped away after the 2024 campaign. The five sued as individuals and did not involve the umpires' union, their lawyer, Paul B. Holmes, said, per the AP.

A pretrial conference in the case is scheduled for Dec. 11.

#2643. Cardinals’ biggest mistake at 2026 NFL Trade Deadline

Cardinals' biggest mistake at 2026 NFL Trade Deadline appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Arizona Cardinals had already signaled that they were prepared to turn the page on their struggling 2026 campaign. Trading Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jacoby Brissett showed that general manager Monti Ossenfort was willing to sacrifice established talent for future draft capital. Yet, when the trade deadline arrived, Arizona suddenly became reluctant to part with two of its most valuable veterans. This left the Cardinals with a missed opportunity to accelerate their rebuild. For a team sitting near the bottom of the NFC West, holding onto valuable assets could prove more costly than letting them go.

Sitting at 3-6 and anchored to the bottom of the NFC West, Arizona's 2026 campaign has unraveled under first-year head coach Mike LaFleur. The Cardinals opened with an encouraging road victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, but three consecutive defeats quickly exposed their defensive vulnerabilities. They later bounced back with hard-fought wins over the Rams and Dallas Cowboys, only to lose to Denver and Seattle. Arizona's defense has surrendered 28.3 points per game. Injuries have devastated the offense. Left tackle Paris Johnson Jr., running back Jeremiyah Love, wide receiver Michael Wilson, and quarterback Gardner Minshew II have all landed on Injured Reserve. With Carson Beck now taking over at quarterback, the franchise has little reason to prioritize short-term results over long-term roster construction.

That reality makes Ossenfort's inaction on deadline day particularly puzzling. Arizona had already demonstrated a willingness to accumulate draft capital. Trading Harrison to Houston for a 2027 second-round pick and a seventh-round selection, while sending a 2027 sixth-rounder to the Texans. The Cardinals also dealt Brissett to Baltimore for a 2027 fourth-rounder and a 2028 seventh-round pick. And yet, Baker and Sweat remained in Arizona after the November 10 deadline.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Baker was arguably the biggest missed opportunity. The Buffalo Bills reportedly made a compelling offer for the veteran safety. Arizona ultimately held firm. Buffalo pivoted to Tennessee's Amani Hooker. They acquired him for a second-round pick while receiving a fifth-rounder in return. Reports indicated that the Cardinals viewed Baker as the emotional heartbeat of the franchise and were reluctant to move him.

There is certainly a human element to that decision. Baker has been a franchise icon and one of the most recognizable faces of the organization. At the same time, sentimentality cannot become a substitute for sound roster management. At 30, Baker remains a valuable player. Still, Arizona cannot assume his trade value will remain this high indefinitely. A premium Day 2 selection could have helped address several positions of need, particularly with the roster facing a substantial rebuild.

Sweat presented another opportunity. The edge rusher had generated legitimate trade chatter. ESPN identified him as a prominent potential deadline candidate. His contract situation complicated the market, though. He reportedly wanted a new deal and that acquiring teams would have to account for his financial commitments. Still, Arizona should have explored whether a contender was willing to make an offer worth accepting. Even if the return fell short of what the Cardinals wanted, listening seriously to the market would have been consistent with their rebuilding timeline.

Keeping both veterans leaves Arizona with a difficult balancing act. Baker can still provide leadership and stability for their defense. Sweat, meanwhile, offers a proven pass-rushing presence when available. Still, those contributions must be weighed against the opportunity to acquire draft picks that could help build a younger, deeper roster.

The Cardinals are already dealing with significant injuries and uncertainty at quarterback. Beck's development should be a priority. Their offensive line and receiving corps need considerable attention as well. Additional premium selections would give Ossenfort more flexibility to address those weaknesses rather than relying exclusively on free agency or later-round development.

The Cardinals did not have to trade every veteran or completely dismantle their locker room. However, they needed to recognize that their mounting injuries and quarterback transition made future assets particularly valuable. The Harrison and Brissett deals established a sensible direction. Failing to follow through with Baker and Sweat left that strategy unfinished.

Arizona may still revisit those conversations in the offseason. That said, the deadline represented a rare opportunity to negotiate with contenders facing immediate needs. Ossenfort passed on that chance. For a franchise trying to build its next competitive core, that hesitation could be the Cardinals' biggest mistake of the 2026 season.
